RONALD A. SHEROD
The Grand Master of Masons in California, Most Worshipful Ronald A.
Sherod, was born in Omaha, Nebraska, on May 24, 1926. A descendant of
early settlers of that prairie state, he came to California when he was only
sixteen.
He attended Wilson High School in Long Beach, and then enlisted in
the United States Navy during World War II . During that conflict he served
his country as a Navy Pharmacist Mate. Honorably discharged in 1945, he
enrolled at the University of California, Los Angeles, where he received a
Bachelor of Science Degree in Higher Accounting in 1950.
Professionally, our Grand Master is a licensed Certified Property
Manager, Public Accountant, and Real Estate Broker. He served as President, and Chief Executive Officer of Equitable Management Corporation
until his retirement in 1985. He is a sought-after consultant in the highly
specialized field of housing for the elderly. He is a nationally recognized
authority and speaker on housing for seniors, and served on the Council on
Aging under President Reagan. In addition, he served on several non-profit
boards such as the California Association for the Homes on Aging.
In June, 1946, he married the former Terry Hennig. They have one son.
Craig, who is an electrical engineer. They are members of the United Church
of Christ, and our Grand Master served as Moderator in his local congregation, as well as the Chairmen of the Board of Deacons for several terms. In
addition, he served for two years as a Director for the Southwest Conference
of the United Church of Christ.
Our Grand Master was Raised on July 22, 1953, in Bixby Knolls-Neptune
Lodge No. 699 in Long Beach, and served as its Master in 1961 . He is also
a member by affiliation with International City Lodge No. 389 in Long Beach.
In 1969 he was appointed Inspector of the 634th Masonic District, and served
in this capacity for three years. In 1977 he was appointed to serve on the
Grand Lodge Committee on Lodge Resources and Development, and in
1980 was appointed a Trustee of the Masonic Homes of California. He
continued to serve as a Homes Trustee for the next ten years until his election
as Grand Master. He also served as a Trustee of the California Masonic
Memorial Temple in San Francisco. and a Trustee of the California Masonic
Foundation.
Brother Sherod is a member of both the Scottish Rite and the York Rite
bodies in Long Beach, and a member of both Al Malaikah and El Bekal Shrine

SUNDAY "PUBLI C AWAREN ESS" DAY
Prior to the opening of Grand Lodge for the transaction of business at
the 142nd Annual Communication, Grand Master Ronald A Sherod had
designated Sunday afternoon, October 13, 1991, as "Public Awareness
Afternoon."
Promptly at 12:30 p.m. a brief ceremony was held to dedicate the new
aluminum flag pole which had been approved for installation in the extreme
northwest corner of the California Masonic Memorial Temple.
Following a prayer by the Very Reverend Joe Jackson, Grand Chaplain,
and brief remarks by Grand Master Sherod, the leaders of our four youth
organizations assisted the Grand Master in raising the flag. Miss Jennifer
Conwell, Grand Worthy Advisor. International Order of Rainbow for Girls in
California, led all in attendance in the Pledge of Allegiance, following which
the Grand Chaplain pronounced the benediction.
All then repaired to the Memorial Temple Auditorium for the balance of
the afternoon program, which consisted of the entrance of the Grand Lodge
Officers with fanfare, welcoming remarks by Grand Master Sherod, and the
presentation of the American Flag by Miss Jennifer Conwell, Grand Worthy
Advisor.
The visiting Grand Masters from sister jurisdictions were received,
accorded Public Grand Honors, introduced by the Grand Marshal and
individually greeted by Grand Master Sherod and Deputy Grand Master
Cazneaux.

REPORT OF THE YOUTH ORDERS COMMITTEE
The Masonic Youth Orders have shown unparalleled enthusiasm, good
fellowship and cooperation this year throughout this jurisdiction. Their
members have been the epitome of Cal ifornia Free Masonry Working
Together. Not surprisingly, it has been the observation of the members of
this Committee that those lodges with thriving Youth Groups are usually the
same lodges that are also thriving, both in membership gains as well as
community involvement. Your Committee speculates that there could very
well be a connection.
Your Committee on Youth Orders continues to have two primary func tions which are; To develop ettective Fraternal relations with the men;ibers
and ad ult leaders of the three Youth Orders and to promote the increase of

6

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

youth programs in the lodges, as well as to encourage the Lodge members
to provide additional adult leadership to their local youth groups.

anyway possible as you plan your Lodge programs for 1992--programs
which will continue to put the YOU in YOUTH.

We are pleased to report that all three Masonic Youth Orders represented by four distinct organizations reported the smallest decline in membership this past year and hopefully the curve will continue to move to the
other end of the scale. They will continue to grow with your help Brethren,
but let us not get complacent with this slight improvement in statistics, for
all four still reported a loss last year. There are Assemblies, Bethels and
Chapters which closed this past year--not for the lack of membership but
for the lack of sufficient number of adult volunteers. Your Committee on
Youth Orders asks that each member of the Grand Lodge here today, return .
to your Temples and seek out a Rainbow Mother Advisor, or Job's Bethel
Guardian or DeMolay Chapter Dad and tell them you want to be involved.

We continued the Lodge Youth Coordinator Program in an effort to
increase the lines of communication between your Lodges and your local
Youth Groups.

7

The Committee held three meetings this year inAnaheim and Sacramento as well as here this morning.

In addition to the increased visitation of the members of this committee,
to both the constituent Lodges and the Youth Groups. other accomplishments were also noticed.

Our membership referral program and accompanying article in the June
issue of California Freemasonry magazine coincided with the Grand Masters
proclamation of Masonic Youth Month. The program seeks the help from
all 150,000 Master Masons in this jurisdiction to refer at least one nonMasonic youth relation or acquaintance for membership in one of the three
Masonic Youth Orders. In the two years we have attempted this program,
just over two hundred referrals have been forwarded to the respective Adult
Leaders.

Over 1000 congratulatory letters were mailed to every DeMolay who
turned 21 in 1991, these letters were signed by your Grand Master and their
primary message was one of good wishes on their journey through adulthood as well as a reminder that should they ever seek additional knowledge
about our beloved fraternity, they need only ask the nearest Master Mason.

Two years of meetings and planning have finalized the qualifications for
the Grand Masters Youth Service Award, and we have finalized the design
and production of the medallion to be worn by those recipients chosen by
the Grand Master to receive the award. It will be the highest award a Master
Mason can receive for his devotions to our Masonic Youth Orders.

Our annual publication of Masonic Orientated Scholarships was completed in March of this year and suitable quantities were distributed through
the Adult leaders of the Youth Groups as well as through the members of
this Committee at our visitations.

Your committee on Youth Orders is pleased to report that it also
represented your Grand Lodge at the following events:

In August, the annual MAYO (Masonic Adults of the Youth Orders)
meeting between the Adult Leaders of the four Youth Organizations and the
members of the Executive Committee was held under the auspices of the
Youth Orders Committee and served as an open forum for all attending to
share and discuss mutual areas of concern as well as ideas for growth and
prosperity. It was most pleasing this year to notice the first time ever that
all Executive Grand Line Officers as well as all Adult Leaders were able to
attend.
As in past years. this committee has prepared an information package
for all Senior Wardens and we urge the Brethren to visit our booth on G floor
and pick up your packets. Our Committee members, staffing the booth, are
most anxious to answer your questions and are willing to assist you in

Your Committee will continue to address itself to its goals and purposes
as well as the Masonic Youth Organizations membership declines in the
1992 Masonic year.
Finally, I must inject a personal note. Having served this committee for
the past seven years, with the greatest of personal pleasure and satisfaction.
Having seen it prosper and grow to the largest Committee in this Grand
Lodge (as well it should be considering our charge). and being a firm believer
that new leadership injects new ideals and goals to be reached (which is
vital to the survivorship of any organization), I have asked not to be
re-appointed as Chairman in 1992, but to return to the ranks in some other
capacity.
I leave this assignment with a deep feeling of gratitude for having had a
hand in helping to shape and direct the policies and programs of this
Committee and I shall certainly continue to support them to the fullest extent
of my ability. I also leave with some regrets that not all of our goals laid
down by our D.G.M. in 1988 have been reached, but my faith in my
successor relieves this anxiety, and I am confident that this Committee will
continue to take great strides in the future, and that our Masonic Youth will
ultimately be served.
I wish to express my sincere gratitude to each of the Grand Masters
under whom I have had the pleasure of serving. My thanks also to the Very
Worshipful Robert A. Klinger, Grand Secretary and to his exceptional Grand
Lodge office staff for their wonderful cooperation. My sincere appreciation
also goes to the many enthusiastic and dedicated members of this Committee with whom I have had the pleasure of working with over the years and
especially to the many adult leaders of the Youth Orders whose help and
cooperation have been invaluable.
But most of all, and best of all, to the members of the Masonic Youth
Orders--Thank you, it's been great-we're on a roll-let's keep it moving
forward and never look back.
Respectfully submitted ,

Most Worshipful Grand Master, Brethren, Ladies and Friends, it is
indeed a pleasure to have this opportunity to tell you about the California
Masonic Foundation, the work we are doing to promote Masonic charity,
and to report to you on the achievements made during the past year.
The California Masonic Foundation was established in 1969 by the
Grand Lodge as a non-profit charitable corporation under the laws of the
State of California, for the furtherance of all phases of education, charitable
and scientific purposes. The Foundation was initially funded by the
proceeds from the sale of the Masonic Club houses adjacent to the campus
of the University of California at Berkeley and Los Angeles. The proceeds
from this sale of approximately $850,000, established the General Fund and
the interest earned from the investment of these funds were and still are
disbursed in the form of scholarship awards to college level students
through out the state. As a recognized charitable corporation within the
State of California the scholarships are awarded on the basis of financial
need without bias to race or religion. In 1972, the Order of Amaranth
conveyed a trust fund of approximately $220,000 to the foundation in token
of their support of the Foundation's scholarship program. The Order of the
Amaranth has yearly added to this original contribution and the Foundation
is grateful for their continued support. To date, scholarsh ips exceeding

12

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

$250,000 have been distributed from the interest earned on the Amaranth
Fund.

The Foundation has endeavored to maintain a balance between quality
and quantity of the scholarship awards. Current Scholarships are generally
awarded yearly in the amount of $1000 per year. This represents essentially
$4000 benefit to the student who maintains acceptable scholastic status. In
the last couple of years, the Foundation has distributed over $100,000 in
scholarships to approximately 1oo students all over the state. Applications
for scholarships far exceed the current capability of the Foundation but the
committee does its best to make equitable judgements so that the most
deserving are properly recognized .

In recent years. several categories of scholarship funds have been
established to acknowledge special considerations of major donors. These
conditions may be geographical (such as students whose residences are in
specific locality), unique qualifications (such as for students who excel in
sports, or youth group activities, ect.), or students studying specific subjects. These funds are typically designated , according to the donors wishes,
by a specified name with all monies separately recorded and accounted.
Awards are made recognizing the specific fund and in accordance with the
specific conditions established. At present the separate Funds administered by the Foundation include the following: The Amaranth Fund,
the Robinson Fund, the Lister Fund, The Starr King Lodge Fund, The
Coalinga Masonic Fund, the Mackechnie Fund, and the McElwain Fund. In
addition, a Grand Masters Fund and a Chowchella Lodge Fund are in the
process of being established . Discussions have been initiated with Soquel
Masonic Lodge which it is hoped will also initiate a new Fund.
Donations, bequests, and contributions received by the Foundation
from individuals, foundations and estates of decedents have contributed
materially to the scope of the awards and grants which are distributed. Many
Lodges and individuals have adopted the Foundation Scholarship Fund as
the charity of choice for memorial donations and honorariums. Such
contributions, bequests, and donations are actively sought by the Trustees
so that the scope of activities may continue to be broadened. The Foundation is indebted to those who have contributed during this past year; your
continued support is greatly appreciated .
The present Foundation endowment totals in excess of $2,000,000.
These funds are conservatively invested by the Investment Committee of
Grand Lodge and the Foundation yearly distributes the interest earned for
its charitable programs. This way each of the separate Funds are a preputial
and potentially increasing resource.
The concept of living Trusts has created a major source of potential
future funds for the Foundation. The Foundation has recently been named
the beneficiary in several major living trusts and in the next few years could
easily double its current endowment. Brother Earald H. Barton and Brother
Carl Graves have established living trusts with the California Masonic Foundation as beneficiaries. The ultimate receipt of these funds could substantially increase the Foundation's resources and the magnitude of the
scholarship program.

13

Application for scholarships may be obtained by written request to the
California Masonic Foundation in care of Grand Lodge. Masonic youth are
really encouraged to apply for these scholarships.
The interest occurring from the General Fund again provided $8,000 to
aid the Masonic youth groups with their leadership training. This program
has proved to be most beneficial and is particularly rewarding for the
Foundation.
While the scholarship program has been the single thrust of the foundation since its creation, in 1988 the Foundation had matured to the point
where it could expand its influence and perform a major educational and
charitable service to society. Under the leadership of Most Worshipful Leo
Mark, the Foundation undertook the support of the Grand Lodge's "Drug
and Alcohol Abuse Educational Program". President Bush's initiative on the
"War Against Drugs" clearly needs the help, aid, and assistance of all
concerned citizens - we must all do all we can to conquer this extreme threat
to our nation. The Foundation clearly sees this as a great opportunity to
solicit the help of the friends of our fraternity to join with us to provide
assistance to the drug and alcohol abuse educational programs in the
schools in our state. The Grand Lodge's program is operated through the
superintendents of the ten state school districts and provides Masonry with
the vehicle to directly participate in this battle. You can not pick up a
newspaper without seeing several articles which define the magnitude of the
Drug and Alcohol Abuse problem throughout the United States. The
menace of illegal drugs requires all concerned citizens to join together to
provide an integrated multi-fronted attack. The time has come for Masons
to do everything possible to insure that the entire population will just "SAY
NO TO DRUGS."
The educational program sponsored by the Grand Lodge and administered by the Public Schools Committee is directed at providing educational materials for the junior high and elementary level student and to aid
the professional teaching staff with their efforts to bring the message of drug

14

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

and alcohol abuse to our youth. For the third year in a row, the Foundation
has been able to fund educational programs in each of the ten state school
districts. The school boards are especially grateful for this support and it is
having a very positive impact on the perception of Masonry in California.
This program is clearly recognized by the members of our Fraternity
who contributed over $150,000 in 1989 and about $250,000 in 1990. Over
$200,000 has already been received this year. Please stop by the
Foundation's booth downstairs during these Grand Sessions for more
information on this program.
The goal is to attempt to raise $500,000 each year to fund this most
important program. The Foundation is currently working on next year's
program, and it is hoped that each of you will enthusiastically support this
noble effort and include a fund raising activity: maybe as part of your Lodge's
public schools program. The financial objectives of this program can not
be reached solely by the solicitation of contributions from the Brethren. The
Foundation is working to create an appeal to the public and establish a
comprehensive fund raising program with the support of all segments of our
communities. Read the "Freemason" for developments as this program
progresses. Find where your respective Lodges can help - let'sletthe public
know of the "good works we Masons perform".
This has been a rewarding time for the Foundation and the message is
reaching the membership. The Board is especially grateful to Most Worshipful Ronald A. Sherod for his enthusiastic support this year. The Trustees
are dedicated to the continuation of the momentum and enthusiasm created
within the Board Members during the past few years. The Trustees are
dedicated to discharge their responsibilities to the Masons of this Grand
Jurisdiction in a most responsible manner and are appreciative of the
opportunity to serve. We have a big challenge before us but one which if
executed with diligence will demonstrate the contributions Masons make to
the world around us. Thank you.
Respectively submitted,
Donald C. Briggs, President

GRAND ORATIO N
"Build Well!"
It's been quite a year. When the Most Worshipful Grand Mast_er first
asked me if I would serve as one of his appointive Grand Lodge Offlc.ers, I
had absolutely no idea what it would entail, but I said yes anyway. As 1t.has
turned out, I've never regretted my decision. I hope that Most Worshipful
Brother Sherod hasn't regretted asking --- at least not too often.
After preparing the first couple of orations, I discovered a totally unexpected benefit of my responsibilitie~. I was thinking mo.re about ~-aso~ry
than I had done since when I was trying to learn my candidate prof1c1enc1es
back in 1981, and as a result. I started to develop a better ans~er, at least
for me, to the question of what it means to be a Mason. I believe th.at my
answer has validity for everyone. even if only as a basis for further discussion. Freemasons are builders.
The Freemasons of today are the spiritual descendants of the Gothic
architects of the European middle ages. Those highly skilled builde~s of _the
magnificent stone cathedrals of Gothic archit~cture were th~ historical
forerunners of our fraternity. The Master builders, the architects who
designed those structures , were indeed a closely knit fraternity of respected
craftsmen wherever they traveled.
The Freemaso ns of today, however. are not often the act~al a~chitects
or stonemasons. We no longer build with stone, today w_e bu.1ld ~1th much
more enduring materials. The Freemasons of today build with ideas, and
our product is not buildings or cathedrals, but men's minds!
The guilds of Gothic Europe cared for their members. and taug~t t_
hem
to live lives of moral character designed to bring honor to the guild itself
through the actions of the guild's individual me'.11bers. Al~hough the need
for operative stonemasons diminished i~ the ~id to l_
ate sixteenth century.
the need for men of upright character in society did not. Free~sonry
changed from an operative, or working craft. to a speculative. or ph1l osoph1cal organization.
Freemasonry is not a religion. Freemasonry does not claim to be "~
way or~truth , or~life" , just a,way ...a.truth and a.life. We as Freemasons.
whether speaking of Blue Lodge Masons. or Scottish Rite Masons. or York

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Rite Masons, or Shrine Masons, or, for that matter, members of the Order
of the Eastern Star, or the Amaranth, or DeMolay, or Job's Daughters, or
Rainbow Girls. or any organization which is a part of the Masonic Family, -we as Freemasons don't believe that you must be a member of our
organizations in order to live a moral and upright life, just that if you Ara a
member of the Masonic Family, you should live your life in a moral and just
manner.

In all, the Masons of the United States contribute over two and a half
million dollars per day ... each and every day ... to various charitable needs
of society.

16

Neither is Freemasonry some Satanic cult! The Masonic family is
merely a group of individually devout men and women who are striving to
make the entire world a better place for everyone to inhabit.
One of the earliest lessons that a Mason is taught is that to relieve the
distressed is a duty incumbent on all men, but particularly on Masons. Vast
sums of money are contributed by the various Masonic organizations of the
United States to many different charities sponsored by them.
There are the justifiably renown Shrine Crippled Children's Hospitals
and Burn Centers. Over three hundred twenty-five million dollars per year
are spent to maintain these hospitals alone, and no patient ever pays
anything.
The York Rite Masons support the Knight Templar Eye Foundations to
research and treat eye disorders. The Scottish Rite operates its 77
Childhood Language Disorders Oinics, which diagnose and treat such
disorders as Dyslexia and Aphasia, again at absolutely no cost to the patient.
The Grotto has programs which aid the Cerebral Palsy Child and other
programs to provide complete dental care for Handicapped Children. Still
no cost to the patient.
Various other Masonic Medical Research Programs provide support for
the medical community's struggle to find new treatments for, or even better,
cures for such ills of mankind as Muscular Dystrophy, Schizophrenia,
Leukemia, Parkinson's Disease, Heart Disease, Diabetes. geriatric disorders
such as Alzheimer's Disease, Cancer research, Arthritis . .. and on, and on,
and on!
Here in California, this Grand Lodge through its California Masonic
Foundation, has in just three years contributed over $500,000 toward a
program to educate our elementary school children about the dangers of
Alcohol and Drug Abuse, and it appears likely that the Freemasons of
California will contribute about $250,000 more this year!

17

We must remember, however that that $2.5 million figure is reached only
if we consider all donations by all members of the Masonic Fam~y. Our
Masonic Youth Groups, Job's Daughters, DeMolay, Rainbow Girls. The
Eastern Star, York Rite. Scottish Rite, Shrine, Grotto, Sciots, Amaranth,
High-Twelve Clubs ... all these organizations and more. All require ~ither
membership in a Masonic Lodge, or relation to a Mason, or sponsorship by
a Mason. And all of these groups are founded upon the same Masonic moral
and ethical teachings.
Our Masonic teachings inform us, however, that even if we bestow all
our goods to feed the poor ... and have not charity, it profiteth us nothing.
1suggest to you, my friends, that Charity must, therefore, be more than the
mere donation-of-dollars.
The English word "charity'' is derived from the Latin word caritas, which
is also translated as "love." The particular connotation of the translation is
that of Brotherly Love.
The tenet of Brotherly Love, is the concept that the whole human species
should be regarded as one family, (derived from the same source) which,
as inhabitants of the same planet, should aid, support and protect each
other, in order to preserve the world in which we all live, and to unite men
of every country, sect, and opinion. This has been taught to Masons "since
time immemorial" as one of Freemasonry's principal tenets.
I submit to you that Brotherly Love, Relief of the distressed , nonhypocritical Truth of action, are all bound together into a concept that can
be called Charity. It is liQI the giving of money that makes the programs I
described to you charitable. It is the act of endeavoring to assist those who
are afflicted to have the best life possible for them, which has elevated the
aforementioned relief of the distressed to a level which encompasses the
true meaning of Masonic Charity. Let me emphasize that again. It is the
reasoning which induces the donation, which causes that relief to take on
the character of Masonic Charity!
So just where does this "revelation" lead us? Perhaps we must consider
just what difference there is between being "a Mason" and being "Masonic
in character."

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Seated in the East this afternoon, are four very exceptional young men
and women. Skip Wahl and Loren Southard, who are the Jurisdiction Master
Councilors respectively of the Northern and Southern California Jurisdictions of the Order of DeMolay, Miss Sabrina Webb, the Grand Bethel
Honored Queen in California, of the International Order of Job's Daughters,
and Miss Jennifer Conwell, Grand Worthy Advisor in California, of the
International Order of the Rainbow for Girls.

At certain times during our ritual, every Mason is asked two questions.
"Where were you first prepared to be made a Mason?" and "What makes
you a Mason?" We Masons know the answers dictated by ritual. and I am
not permitted to state those answers here today. I do, however, challenge
every Mason to consider, not the words of the ritual, but what is meant by
those words.

Jurisdiction Master Councilors Webb and Southard . I have no doubt
that, when age and circumstances permit, you and those of your DeMolay
Brothers who choose to join our Fraternity, will be welcomed with open arms
to full membership in some Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons, wherever
that Lodge may be located. You and those whom you lead, have overwhelmingly demonstrated your devotion, both personal and as an Order, to
the principles upon which our Fraternity is based.
Grand Bethel Honored Queen Webb. You and your Sisters are our
literal relations. You are our daughters, our Granddaughters, nieces and
sisters. You are. both in fact and by your actions, a part of our Masonic
Family. You, although you are all eligible to be members of the Order of the
Eastern Star, will not ever be members of a Masonic Lodge, yet to those of
us who are members of the Fraternity, you will forever be a part of us.
Grand Worthy Advisor Conwell , --- Jennifer. Because of my involvement
with Rainbow, and my membership on the Rainbow Grand Executive
Committee in California, I have been privileged to get to know you, and many
of your Rainbow Sisters on a personal basis. You and those whom you lead,
are not necessarily related to any Mason in any fashion other than through
your membership in your Order. You, like the Jobs Daughters, will never
be members of a Masonic Lodge, and you may or may not even be eligible
to join the Eastern Star. unless you happen to later in life marry an man who
is or who becomes a Mason. Your organization's connection to Masonry
is the most tenuous of the three Youth Groups, yet your Order's goal of
Service clearly shows all of Rainbow to be Masonic in character.
These three Masonic Youth Groups, and the thousands of members of
those organizations, are not Masons. They are. however, Masonic in
character. The ladies of the Eastern Star aren't Masons either, but the Order
of the Eastern Star is Masonic in character. For that matter, many of the
members of the Salvation Army are not Masons. and the organization itself
is not sponsored by Masons. But I ask you to consider whether, perhaps,
just perhaps. the Salvation Army might also be Masonic in character.

19

I offer now, for your consideration, one interpretation of those ritual
answers. I believe that what makes a person a "Mason", is. in part. that
persons choice to dedicate his or her life to the betterment of the society in
which all of mankind must live.
The Sisters of Love. Religion, Nature, Immortality, Fidelity, Patriotism,
Service of Rainbow. The Five Messengers of Job's Daughters. The Seven
Preceptors of DeMolay. The Star Points of the Eastern Star. Brotherly Love,
Relief, and Truth. Temperance, Fortitude, Prudence, and Justice. Faith ,
Hope, Charity. All of these lessons are the same. even though diverse in
ritualistic presentation. Masonic organizations, however, don't have a
proprietary "lock" on these universal truths. Many organizations, and many
individuals who don't belong to any organization recognize the universality
of these moral and ethical concepts. And the target of these truths is also
the same. The target is some person who in his or her innermost self,
believes that he or she can make a difference.
A healthy society, one which values freedom and healthy growth, can't
exist without certain moral and ethical tenets to support and guide those of
whom it is composed, anymore than a Gothic cathedral could have been
erected in a satisfactory manner without a properly formed and laid
cornerstone to support the stones of which it was built.
Freemasonry, as well as each of its concordant and appendant bodies,
is composed of men and women who have chosen those moral and ethical
tenets to be their guide during their lives. We need not try to convert others
to our way of thinking through words. We need only to live our lives
according to the principles to which we obligated ourselves at the altars of
our various organizations, and by example we will attract those of like mind.
But whether they join one of our Masonic organizations or not, everyone,
--- I repeat, --- everyone who lives their life in accordance with those moral
and ethical concepts which we chose to call "Masonic ideals", is a part of
that "living stone" which serves as the cornerstone of our society.
With apology to our Ritual Committee, I would like to share with you the
mental interpretation which I hear every time I listen to the Master's Benediction which concludes every full form closing of a Masonic Lodge.

May the blessing of Heaven rest upon us and all who live their lives in
accordance with Masonic principles! May the Masonic tenet of Brotherly
Love prevail throughout the world, and every moral and social virtue cement
all who so live tlleir lives! Amen.
My friends, we --- all of us, whether a part of our great Masonic Family
or not --- have the potential to be the moral and ethical cornerstone of the
world in which we live. We --- all of us -- are the builders of the society of
tomorrow in which our children (so wonderfully represented by these Youth
Groups) will live, as well as the builders of the society of today. The future
can't be anything other than what the present builds it to be.

EULOGY
EUGENE S. HOPP, PAST GRAND MASTER
by Donald B. McCaw, Past Grand Master
The poet, Milton, describes death as the "golden key that o pens the
palace of eternity. "
Most Worshipful Eugene S. Hopp, a Master Mason, was one of the
outstanding men of our time: a scholar, a physician, a civic leader, and one
of the great Grand Masters of this jurisdiction. He was well prepared to give
a good account of his stewardship while here on earth and earned his place
in that palace of eternity when he passed to that place not made with hands,
eternal in the heavens on October 19th of last year.
Dr. Hopp was born in the State of New York; he received his Bachelor
of Science degree from the University of Georgia and matriculated to the
Georgia School of Medicine, where in 1937 he earned his Doctorate in
medicine. Our Brother was then selected from among his peers to continue
his Post-Graduate work at prestigious Oxford University on the Thames,
north and west of London.
Volunteering fo r military service in 1937, he later served as Chief of the
Eye, Ear, Nosf) and Throat Service of the 81 st General Hospital in the
European Theater of Operations during 1944 and 1945.
Upon his discharge from the military, he became a civilian consultant
to the Surgeon General of the United States Army and later to the United
States Air Force. He was Commander of San Francisco Chapter of the
Military Orders of World Wars, and a Life Member of American Legion, Rialto
Post No. 203.
Following his arrival in San Francisco, Dr. Hopp became Clinical Professor of Ear, Nose, and Throat disorders at the University of California and
later served as the President of the Staff of Hahnemann Hospital during the
years 1958 and 1959. He was a respected member of the Board of Directors
of the San Francisco Med ical Society and a fellow of the American College
of Physicians and Surgeons, as well as the Royal Society of Medicine in
England. Our Brother was named Professor Emeritus of the California
Med ical College in San Francisco in 1978.
Brother Gene was known for his great ability to retain knowledge and
he possessed a penetrating mind. These abilities earned membership in the

24

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

prestigious Phi Beta Kappa and Phi Kappa Phi Honor Societies. He was an
inventor as well and developed an instrument for the examination of the
larynx. He also received the George Washington Honor Medal Award from
the Freedom Foundation of Valley Forge.

recognizing the worthwhile things of life and then making those
same worthwhile things a part of our personal life.

Most Worshipful Brother Hopp was an author and a valued contributor
to numerous medical and scientific journals. He also was a highly respected
member and Past President of our Masonic Philalethes Society.
Brother Hopp was a member of the San Francisco Bible Breakfast Club,
the Rotary Club, and many other civic and professional organizations,
including the United Crusade of San Francisco, the Commonwealth Club,
and Goodwill Industries, to name a few.
Our Fraternity took particular pride in his long service as Commissioner
of the San Francisco Board of Education during a most difficult social era
in the history of this country and this city in particular; and to his great credit
and to the credit of all Freemasonry, he served as President of that Board
during some of it's most trying times.
Dr. Eugene Hopp was the Master of King Solomon-Seaport Lodge No.
260, which later consolidated with Starr King Lodge No. 344, and served this
jurisdiction with great distinction as it's Grand Master in 1967 and 1968. He
later became a member of Marin Lodge No. 191 in San Rafael.
Above all. Dr. Hopp exemplified the great qualities of men who are
outstanding among us. His character was such that his burdensome tasks
were never too important nor was his schedule too busy to help the less
fortunate. Among his many writings which received wide acclaim, he wrote
about "character" and told us:
"Character is the individual activation of brotherly love, relief and
truth, temperance. fortitude, prudence. justice and more. Character is only effective when it is activated. We can write about
character and we can read about it, but until we activate it, we
remain ordinary and untried . We alone make the personal decision
to develop a greater character for ourselves. or to be satisfied with
the status quo.
Now, character cannot be bestowed, bought or borrowed . It
belongs only to the man who develops it and, like rare wine, it
improves every year. Character is free to those who seek its
improvement for themselves; the effort in no way interferes with our
daily work or relaxation or family time. The effort consists of

25

It is a joy while we are here, happiness for our family; success for
ourselves; and, in the end. it bequeaths to everyone the greatest
wealth of all."
We honor and pay our respects to this man of great character and high
integrity. Those of us whose lives were touched by Dr. Eugene S. Hopp are
better men and women for it. No greater tribute can be paid to his memory.
So mote it be.

NECROLOGY REPORT
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Members of the Grand Lodge:
Since we last assembled here, in the house of the faithful, 502 members
of this Grand Lodge have joined the endless line of splendor of those who
have labored so long and so diligently erecting the Temple of Masonry in
the hearts of men. Their individual names will be inscribed upon the printed
record of this Annual Communication.
As the sur:i has set in the West for them. and they have laid down the
working tools from their tired hands, it is for us who survive them. to take up
those emblematic tools and continue to erect that spiritual building whose
construction never ends.
There is none assembled here who does not cherish the memory of a
Brother Mason who influenced his life for the better. He signed your petition.
he was your coach, he was the Master who raised you: but most of all, he
was a man who set an example which you found worthy of imitation.
These men were by birth, human, by character, gentlemen . by love.
husbands and fathers, and by choice. they were Masons. As Masons. they
were charged to practice the domestic and public virtues, to govern their
llves, their thoughts and their conduct according to the great moral duties
Incumbent upon all who wear the lambskin as the badge of a Mason.

As they were members of this sovereign Grand Lodge, so were they
leaders of Masons as was said of our Ancient Athenian Brethren. "None
served with more honor than these, yet many served and there was much
honor."

Finally, my Brethren, let us honor and eulogize the memory of those
who have passed on the perfection in the most practical and meaningful
way that is possible for us - by exemplifying in our actions those immutable
principles to which they dedicated their lives.

MESSAGE OF THE GRAND CHAPLAIN

The Grand Master instructed the Grand Secretary to send appropriate
letters to the seven Past Grand Masters who were unable to be present at
the Communication.

Years ago, and of course I am now at the age I can say "years ago," I
had the distinct privilege of working with Dr. Orin Whitton minister of
Christian churches here in California. One day he was telling me of a man
he had met who claimed to be an atheist. Dr. Whitton said he asked the
man, "You mean to say that you have no religious beliefs? That in itself is a
strong belief. Or to say that you surmise that. sometime in the past there
was this great explosion and that this rock was hurled out into a vacuum,
started to spin, and now millions of years later we have "Disneyland"? You
really believe there is no plan or greater guidance than man here on earth?"
"Well," said the man, "maybe there is something stronger than just man in
control." "Oh!", then Dr. Whitton said, "you might say that you are an
Agnostic." ''That's it," replied the man. "I'm an Agnostic." "Now we're getting
someplace," replied Dr. Whitton. "What kind of an Agnostic do you believe
you are?" 'What do you mean, 'What kind of Agnos.ti~ am I?'. 1. don't
understand." Then the man was asked if he was a Christian Agnostic or a
Jewish Agnostic, Mohammedan. "What don 't you believe?" Let's say that
from the beginning of time, people were able to record their knowledge, and
of all this knowledge stored in all the books in all the libraries in all the world,
how much of this knowledge do you personally have? Maybe, one tenth of
one hundredth of one percent? Then with just this much knowledge how
can we say something did or did not happen in the past or what is written
Is true or false. Here my friend is where Faith comes in, that which we do
not know we take on faith and with faith comes love and trust, and if we do
not have love and trust, or lets call it faith, we would, as some people do live
behind a wall of mistrust. They fancy th emselves as the "holders of the truth,"
but let me say here loud and clear that love, peace and harmony can only
come from the searchers of the truth, for we find that throughout history,
"The beholders of the truth seem to always want to defend, and sometimes
very violently, this truth that they believe they hold."

that the opposite of love is "Hate." I don't believe that. I believe that the

you have nothing, you just don't care. Apathy is the greatest destroyer of
all our emotions. Apathy can and does destroy friendships, marriages,

As your Grand Chaplain the question of some of the churches anacking
our Fraternity arises quite often in conversations with the Brethren. Because
one of our prerequisites is a belief in God and we give thanks to the almighty
during our assemblies, some make reference to us as a church or a cult,
these are the beholders I referred to in the beginning of my talk. In Masonry
I believe that the reference to God can be best denoted in a quotation from
the writings of John D. Rockefeller where he wrote, "I believe in an all wise
and all loving God, named by whatever name, and that the individuals
highest fulfillment, greatest happiness and widest usefulness are to be found
in living in harmony with his will. As long as we stand by our basic and
fundamental principles of brotherly love relief and truth and practice, out of
the Lodge, those great moral duties which are inculcated in it, this shall be
our shield against any attack from those who would have the world believe
they know what Masonry is all about.
As we look down the road to the future of Masonry, the road may look
a little rough and rugged, and many questions will have to be answered, but,
on the way to finding the answers to our ultimate survival. how often do we
hide behind the skirts of nostalgic comparison of what used to be, or find
our apocalypse solution by the Band-Aid answer of "What we need is more
new members!" (Whatever happened to the old ones?) I don't believe it is
the dream of new members that will save us, nor is it how we were in the
past years that will sustain us. The answer, my Brethren, is in the "Now" ...
you and I ... present and accountable, who will build and strengthen the
Lodges of today and tomorrow. It will only be through active affirmation by
each member that the future of Masonry will be a manifest reality.
Now in conclusion, let me leave you with a little story, "lest we forget
whence we came."
Years ago along the rocky coast of Maine, during the stormy season,
many shipwrecks occurred, and many liv'es were lost. Well, four caring men
came together and agreed to pledge their efforts to try and save as many
of these shipwreck victims as possible. On one of the rocky points they
erected a little lifesaving station, put in a few cots, medical supplies, and a
stove to keep the saviors warm. They bought a boat and agreed that during
the stormy season they would each take turns standing watch, and if a wreck
occurred they would ring the large bell they had erected on the point to
summon the other three. This they did, and were very successful at saving
the li\tes of many who would have surely have drowned. Their notoriety
spread far and wide, and the people said, "This is good, and we must join

Now along that coast in Maine, there are many beautiful Yacht Clubs,
all the lifesaving is hired, and the o riginal intent has been long forgotten . So
my Brethren, may we never forget whence we came or whither we are going,
and may we always remember to give thanks to the memory of those
Brethren who, through their wisdom, not only secured our future, but chose
to preserve and share a moment of their history not only with us here today,
but for future generations. May they be the example which will inspire us to
prepare for our future generations and to share with them a moment of our
times and history.
I truly believe that as long as there are great Fraternal o rganizations such
as ours, whose dedicated members continue to build for a better tomorrow,
and through or by example can influence the continued bu ilding of our great
nation on the foundation of love of God , Country and Family and live a life
of truth and morality, then we can hope to preserve a future where there will
always be ... "One nation under God , indivisible, with liberty and justice for

all."

GRAND MASTER' S MESSAG E

pleased to report the total transition went exceptionally well. The consensus

My Brethren:
As I now conclude my term of office as Grand Master, I am required to
prepare a report to the membership of this Grand Lodge. This is a report
on the condition of Masonry in our jurisdiction and of the many significant
and official acts of this past year of our Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of
Free and Accepted Masons of California. This is not a chronological report
but a summary of the major factors that shaped and molded this past year.
If I were to describe the results of this past year, I would describe the year
as progressive, cooperative, positive and informative.
I would first of all like to express my appreciation for the fine support,
cooperation and encouragement I have received from the general membership this past year. As the chosen leader assumes his place at the altar
each October to take the solemn obligation to uphold the office of Grand
Master, he is at once beset with a great sense of duty and responsibility.
Such were my precise feelings as I knelt at that altar a year ago on October
10, 1990.
Time passes so very quickly as Lodge and community events come and
go. Decisions, both great and small. besiege a Grand Master on a daily
basis just as would be expected of the operations of any large business such
as our Grand Lodge. The goal is to arrive at a just and equitable solution
that best serves the total family of Freemasonry. As Grand Master, I have
tried to maintain an equitable balance between the many entities of
Freemasonry throughout this past year. It has been my approach to look
for the long term rather than interim solutions. This philosophy has faithfully
supported my theme for California in the year 1991 of "California Masonry .. .Working Together." In retrospect, I can say this philosophy has been
most beneficial to all of Freemasonry as I have faithfully tried to administer
your affairs with a due regard for all concerned. Accordingly, I can say with
great pride that, for the most part, peace and harmony prevails within the
Fraternity. This is a result of a mutual respect and support by all leaders of
the several concordant and appendant bodies of Masonry.
WORKING TOGETHER AS A TEAM
The year 1991 was destined to be a year of extremes as the 'tenure rule"
forced upon us the need to immediately replace about thirty-six Inspectors,
eighteen chairmen and approximately ninety additional committeemen.
This was accomplished with the exception of two Inspectors who, for
specific and logical reasoning, could not be replaced at that time. I am

39

It is my firm conviction that the Grand Master, as well as all the officers
of Grand Lodge, need to be in more direct contact with our membership.
we need to spend more time with the general membership; we need to
establish a line of continuing communication that keeps them advised of the
many activities of Grand Lodge. This was accomplished, in part, by my
monthly Grand Master's Newsletter as it relayed matters of general interest,
including our monthly Itinerary that provides the Lodges with the awareness
of when Grand Lodge would be in their area performing a ceremony or
attending a reception. I am most pleased for the favorable remarks I have
received regarding my Newsletter and how the Masters have benefitted from
my monthly messages. Furthermore , the receiving of the monthly Itinerary
has produced a marked improvement in membership attendance at Grand
Lodge openings and at cornerstones. Effective communication is too often
taken for granted both by Grand Lodge as well as the individual Lodge. The
lack of effective communication continues to be our worst enemy in any
endeavor. not just Masonry.
Shrine Potentates support and cooperation this year has been most
rewarding to this Grand Master! A few of the California Shrine Potentates
were compelled. for economic reasons, to adopt a reasonable, dignified and
low key advertising campaign in early summer. Following my personal
request they graciously ceased advertising in support of my Recommendation on advertising and in the interest of friendship and respect to my office.
During this year I have found that quiet reasoning, understanding and
compassion has worked most favorably for all within this great Fraternity of
Masons. During this year, I have enjoyed an excellent relationship with every
Potentate as well as the Imperial Shrine officers. Such was my good fortune
that these Shrine Brothers were understand ing Masons, willing to work
together for the common benefit of a stronger Masonry.
Imperial Shrine sessions were held this year in San Francisco in the first
week of July. It was my good fortune to be the host Grand Master and the
guest of the Imperial Potentate for that Session. As such. it provided me an
oousual opportunity to become better acquainted with many of their key
leaders and to discuss. in person, my program for Masonic unity. It certainly
prOllided your Grand Master the opportunity for a "front row" seat in the
deliberations and actions of that Imperial Session!

In June, I was extended the privilege of an invitation by their Most

religious services and to address their informal session. Allowing for the
restrictive nature of our California Masonic Code, I was advised by my

as Grand Master, should they be forthcoming. That will allow him to further
the planning of a long term and favorable relationship between the two
organizations.
BUDGETARY CONSTRAINTS
Each of the several Masonic Bodies continue to experience major
budgetary problems as they relate to operating expenses. During this past
year I cannot recall a single Masonic Order that has not personally expressed deep concern for the negative fiscal impact of the high costs of their
operations. Your Grand Lodge is no exception. This past year we have
been able to contain our expenditures in most every category. To insure
full control of all committee expenditures, this past May, I imposed a
moratorium on all non-essential expenditures to soften the heavy cash flow
burdens facing your Grand Treasurer. This is a negative cash flow problem
our Grand Lodge faces near1y every year due to the timing ot the individual
Lodge payments of their per capita assessment.
With these known fiscal problems. I decided before becoming Grand
Master, that I would adopt as many cost saving opportunities as is practical.
This was partially accomplished through adjusting and reducing the re·
quired schedules of Grand Lodge officers. As such, it saved considerably
on the hotel expenses immediately following the close of the last Annual

41

It was my firm intention to reach as many of our members as possible.
and yet remain within reasonable fiscal limitations of approved budgetary
constraints. I accomplished precisely those goals. This past year I combined several cornerstone events by having two or more in a given day.
AccOrdingly, we were able to reduce our Grand Lodge openings that directly
impact our operating budget. On at least one occasion. I was able to lay
the cornerstone without benefit of a Grand Lodge opening. Such an
opportunity does not often present itself nor is it often appropriate.

CONFERENCE OF GRAND MASTERS
It was my distinct honor and pleasure to serve the Conference of Grand
Masters of North America this past year as its National Conference Chairman. California has never been host to the North American Conference of
Grand Masters. Following nearly four years of planning, it became a reality
this past February, in San Diego. I am pleased to report that it was a positive
and valuable Conference. It was an enormous challenge as well as very
time consuming to plan for sixty-two incumbent Grand Masters, numerous
Deputies and Grand Wardens and their wives. With the tremendous support
of many San Diego Masons and their wives this three day annual meeting
was unofficially proclaimed as one of the most outstanding annual meetings
of this illustrious gathering. Concurrently, the Grand Secretaries held their
annual meeting. In all, over eight hundred attended and participated in this
Annual Conference. I should like to take this opportunity to express my
gratitude to M.W. Stanley L. Channon and his outstanding San Diego
committee that provided for all of our guests' every need.

WARDENS' RETREATS
Once again'. the Wardens' Retreats have proven to be a huge success.
These Retreats are limited to one hundred participants and their wives. This
Insures a more "personal" relationship between the participants and their
Instructors. It also provides better opportunities for the elective Grand
Lodge officers and their wives to meet and share ideas with the Wardens.
This being the third year of this excellent program we continue to hear the
Wardens wives remarking that "as a result of the Retreat, they now feel more
self assured in their role as the wife of a Master." The basic purpose of the
Retreat, of course, is to provide the much needed administrative training
that will ultimately prepare the officer to be Master. The Junior Wardens'
Retreats, started last year, provides a unique curriculum designed to address the administrative problems associated w ith their coming year as
Senior Warden. We are most pleased with the enthusiastic support for these
weekend Retreats from the Wardens. At first. it seems expensive to the
attendee because of the requ irement to stay in the hotel for the Retreat. By
so doing, they quickly become an integral part of a unified group, contributing much more in d iscussion than they would have had they been allowed
to return home for the night. Each year th e program improves based on
findings within the classroom environment. Each year the Warden comes
away better prepared to be an effective Master of his Lodge.

MASONIC LEADERS

It became quite apparent to many that we must again remove this
Brother from his office as Master. At the written request of the District
Inspector, and with the verbal support of the Assistant Grand Lecturer, I so
notified this Brother of his immediate removal from office and the interim
appointment to the Master's chair of the Senior Warden. This decision came
as a result of discussions with the members of the Jurisprudence Committee
and the acceptance of their recommendations for resolving this problem.

We are a very large jurisdiction, composed of a membership of nearly
140,000 Masons. Our territory extends nearly eight hundred miles North to
South. With such a geographic challenge, it is certainly understandable that
we, at times, fail to effectively communicate. It has long been my philosophy
that most problems are reduced, or even eliminated, when all parties meet
to discuss the issue and to reach amicable solutions that benefit all parties.
It was because of this philosophy that I formed the Council of California
Masonic Leaders that is now attended by more than thirty-five leaders of all
the concordant and appendant organizations of Freemasonry. All of them
realize the absolute need to put into practice my theme of "California
Masonry... Working Together." This year we have met to discuss key issues
of mutual interest a total of three times. Nearly every Masonic organization
is represented in this very important Council. If it can avoid one
misunderstanding or help to resolve one major issue, for any organization,
it will more than serve its purpose.
DECISIONS
Often times the Grand Master is confronted with a problem that is not
clearly or specifically covered within the California Masonic Code. Or, the
problem is such that he must reach a decision based upon personal
judgment and instinct. What may seem appropriate at the time may later
appear questionable to others. However, th e decision must be made at that
time. Fortunately, this past year has been relatively easy regarding
decisions of this magnitude. Most inquiries were within the scope of the
California Masonic Code. All my decisions were considered and supported
within the general framework of our Code. The following are those actions
requiring the Grand Master's attention.
Decision No. 1: Was for the removal of a Master for failure to comply
with the District Inspector and Assistant Grand Lecturer directives as it
related to the Installation of Officers of his Lodge. In the belief of an improved
attitude by the Master, and at the request of the Assistant Grand Lecturer as
well as the District Inspector, I reinstated this Master following his unequivocal assurance to conform with the duties and responsibilities of his elected
office. However, following his personal assurance and his subsequent
reinstatement. he did not attend Lodge meetings or the District Inspector's
Schools of Instruction, as required by our Code. During his several months
of reinstatement he did not make Lodge committee appointments and was
not available either in person or by telephone to the officers of his Lodge.

4S

Decision No. 2: Was predicated on the highly unusual and irregular
circumstances surrounding the 1972 suspension of a member and the
written request by his Lodge for full reinstatement. Following our review, I
complied favorably to that request. I did so following the advice of the
Chairman on Jurisprudence. With the authority to place this matter now
before· the Lodge, their vote was taken and the vote was unanimous for
reinstatement.
Decision No. 3: Based on the recommendation of the Committee for
the Recognition of Foreign Grand Lodges, as well as the earlier recognition
by the Conference of Grand Masters, I granted interim recognition to four
Grand Lodges in Brazil -- the Grand Lodges of Mato Grosso, Rio Grande
Norte, Roraima, and Sergipe. Again, following investigation and recommendations of our Committe·e, interim recognition was granted to the newly
reconstituted Grand Lodge of Yugoslavia. Two other Eastern European
reconstituted Grand Lodges have sought recognition from the Grand Lodge
of California. ·They will be mentioned in the report of our Committee on
Recognition of Foreign Grand Lodges.
RECOMMENDATIONS
Recommendation No. 1
Eliminating Proflciency Requirement - Third Degree
In 1953, our jurisdiction determined that it was appropriate to require a
Master Mason to commit to memory a major portion of the Master Mason
Degree. This was to occur before he could apply for membership in a
concordant or appendant Masonic organization. In the nearly four decades
since that became law, there is strong reason to believe that it has worked
counter productive to it's intended purpose. Accordingly, it is my recommendation that we should repeal Section 2635 in its entirety. This will
eliminate the· existing requirement for a Third Degree proficiency.

46

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Recommendation No. 2
Relief on Fraternal Advertising
When Section 2072 of our Code was adopted, it was accomplished as
a reaction to the sometimes improper use of advertising within our Craft. It
is my opinion, as well as that of many others, that we may have allowed
ourselves to react too severe and thus deprived ourselves and the concordant and appendant organizations of much needed revenue to support our
fraternal operations. It is my firm opinion that Section 2072 must be revised
to allow our Craft Lodges to accept certain types of advertising to defray the
costs of publishing Lodge Trestleboards. In most instances the cost of
publishing and mailing the Lodge Trestleboard is the single most expensive
item of the Lodge's annual operating budget. This certainly impacts the
Lodge dues structure.
Specific categories of advertising that are excluded are defined in Sub
Sections a. through g. of the Recommendation. Of equal importance to the
passage of this recommendation is that it will then permit all other Masonic
organizations to address their advertising needs, within due bounds, without
impact of the California Masonic Code. It is my hope and I am presuming
that the passage of this Recommendation will not cause a violation of our
California Civil Code nor otherwise place in jeopardy the non-profit status
that the Fraternity is privileged to enjoy

Recommendation No. 3
Cost Impact of Adopted Resolutions
It is my opinion that we must also consider the cost impact of the
adoption of a Resolution or Recommendation before we adopt it. The
budget impact must be considered at the time of the vote. If a Resolution
or Recommendation is adopted, it probably will impact the per capita for the
ensuing year. Therefore, it is my recommendation that Sections 500, 1218
and 4000 of our Masonic Code be amended to require all submitted
legislative matters to have first published the "cost impact" value of that piece
of legislation. The Grand Secretary shall then incorporate that cost estimate
as a part of the total Resolution packet to be distributed to the Lodges as
prescribed by the California Masonic Code.

Recommendation No. 4
Requirement tor Submission of Resolutions
I am deeply concerned with the ever increasing number of Resolutions
and other items of legislation coming before this Grand Lodge at our Annual
Communication. With the very li mited available time to accomplish our

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

47

business at Grand Lodge, it is imperative we seek ways to reduce our
deliberations to only those matters of business that serve the majority of the
Fraternity and not for a very isolated purpose. Over the past few years
several thoughts have been explored to impose a form of control over the
quantity of submissions. To me, that is not equitable as we must be
responsive to all lawful legislation. Over the years, many Resolutions have
been submitted by only one member. For example, this year we have a total
of thirteen Resolutions submitted by only one member and another fourteen
by two members. In all, this represents 66% of the total 1991 submissions
of Resolutions with 31 % of the total being submitted by only one member.
As a comparison, of the four largest jurisdictions in North America, we found
that their total Resolutions submitted, combining all three jurisdictions
averaged a remarkable low number of ten Resolutions per year. California
reports the smallest membership of those four top jurisdictions even though
we far outstrip them in proposed legislation.
My Recommendation proposes that if an intended piece of legislation
is worthy of adoption. it should then contain more than one persons'
endorsement before submission. In effect, my Recommendation No. 4, if
adopted. will require the endorsement of three Grand Lodge members that
are members of at least three separate Lodges. This will further insure that
a Resolution is not representative of "special interests or frivolous legislation."
PUBLIC AWARENESS SUNDAY
The Public Awareness Program for 1991 is now history. Time will tell if
it was a worthwhile venture. Part of the problem within Freemasonry is the
lack of understanding by the general public of "what Masons do" and "what
Masons represent. " We "go public" only at cornerstones, installations and
funerals. Certainly not enough exposure to effectively communicate the
story of Freemasonry! To expand public knowledge about our Fraternity, I
set aside this past Sunday, just before our Communication. to invite the
Mason and non-Masons to share in and experience the several events that
demonstrate our values as a Fraternity. In addition to the visitation to Union
City in the morning, I have brought together in that afternoon's events the
four youth leaders to present their wonderful remarks. These outstanding
youth leaders were then followed by the Grand Oration. Then we invited the
. visiting Grand Masters of other jurisdictions and the visiting leaders of the
several Concordant and Appendant Bodies to participate . This
demonstrated our Fraternity's continuing dedication to supporting the youth
of America and our American right for a free education. We have now
publicly highlighted many of our worthy charities that benefit not. only
Freemasons but the community in general. A short report on the scholar-

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

ship program of the California Masonic Foundation was also presented to
further demonstrate our educational support.

Several jurisdictions have accepted change in the handling of their
candidate memorization requirements. Nebraska, as an example, three
years ago reduced their requirements for candidate memorization to an
absolute minimum. For years they were on the decline in membership. It
may have been coincidental but from the first year of the reduction of
memorization requirements, Nebraska has reported an increase in membership. Even though three years is not a substantial trend it is nevertheless
worth noting and it is reasonable to assume it will continue to prosper
primarily due to the reduction of the memorization demands on the candidate. Other jurisdictions that have taken similar action also are reporting
growth patterns in membership.

CONDITION OF OUR GREAT MASONIC JURISDICTION
We have traveled this jurisdiction into every corner of this huge state.
We visited those very difficult places to reach as well as metropolitan areas
that demand the most of everyone to simply survive the heavy and frantic
traffic. We saw Lodges that were flourishing and we saw Lodges barely
holding on because they offer little or no leadership. A cursory analysis of
the Lodges these new members are joining are those Lodges providing an
energetic and innovative program for their members. The Lodges that are
simply going through the motions are not receiving applications. Our net
membership loss for this past year stands at 5,807 that reduces our revised
membership to 139,511 members. This is a reported 4.1% net membership
loss for this past year. It might be of interest to note that over the past four
years our average annual membership loss was exactly 4.1 %.
We continue to lose members through the usual cause of death and
relocation. However, it is my opinion , and others, that a definite resurgence
is being felt throughout our jurisdiction. Many Lodges this year are reporting
a back log of degree work. Furthermore, many of the new members are in
the "under forty" category. Other jurisdictions are reporting similar findings.
Consolidations continue, as of this writing, with a total of eighteen for
this past year. Predictably, several of these consolidations will prove successful and several will continue to decline regardless of the consolidation.
It is my opinion that consolidations can be effective but only if the merging
Lodges are willing to work as a unit and not as two or more Lodges
suspicious and in competition with each other.
For many years, membership in Freemasonry, in nearly every jurisdic·
tion, has been on the decline. Many ideas have been introduced to stop this
erosion, but without substantial effect. Each year, our "average age" slightly
increases as more members pass away. Throughout our vast Fraternity of
Freemasonry we hear the cry that 'We are not attracting the younger men
to the Fraternity and when we do, we can't hold on to them." In my opinion,
these statements are factual. We are a Nation with a mind for "instant
solutions." There are no "quick fix" solutions to our Masonic decline. There
is no single solution. There is no easy answer. However, in my several years
of intensive travels, I find a strong parallel between Lodge growth and simple
hard work by the Master and his members.

49

Last year, at our Annual Communication, we voted by a very narrow
margin to carry over Resolution No. 90-26 that addresses the issue of
reducing the candidate memorization requirements. The Ritual Committee
has a Resolution before us this year that continues their endorsement of
90·26 but, if passed, asks for the specific "posturing" of the examinee for
stronger emphasis. The Long Range Planning Committee has before us
Resolution No. 90-01 that also reduces the memorization requirements but
recommends several questions and a memorized response. The important
thought here is that most everyone recognizes the urgent need to reduce
the required memory work of a candidate, if we are to attract new members.
Now, it is up to you and me to get the job done! As Grand Master, I heartily
endorse the support of such an important change. My experience shows
clearly that our present system of memorization is not accomplishing it's
Intended results of properly educating the candidates. Unquestionably, it
is surely defeating the desire to join the Fraternity for many very good men.
RITUAL
This year has been an outstanding year of cooperation and support in
all matters pertaining to ritual. As issues are addressed that clearly affect
the Craft, the Ritual Committee has carefully and objectively addressed all
aspects of the issue at hand. Areas that cl early affect the Fraternity, the
Grand Lecturer or a member of his Committee has thoroughly discussed
the subject with the Grand Master to insure his support and to receive his
thoughts on the matter. I have truly appreciated this open line of communication that has been most effective for all concerned.
Throughout this past year, in working with and observing the Ritual
Committee's vast and sometimes clouded areas of duty and responsibility,
I have formulated the following o pinion:

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

It is most important for our widely spread jurisdiction to maintain a
uniformity of our ritual at all times. Considering the physical size of our many
Lodges and the colloquial needs of a given region, it is critical that all
decisions on ritual, as pertaining to floor work, be at the sole discretion of
the Ritual Committee. Voting on the floor of Grand Lodge on many of these
matters cannot effectively insure what is best for the total Fraternity. Only
the Ritual Committee possesses the necessary understanding to insure the
best handling of floor work throughout this vast jurisdiction. No one Lodge
or even a total Division can clearly understand the appropriate needs for the
total jurisdiction.

incoming Grand Master will consider the text of that report sufficient to
submit as a Grand Master's Recommendation. California is looked upon
throughout the North American Conference as a jurisdiction of dignified,
effective and precise floor work. Let's keep it that way .
LONG RANGE PLANNING
Your Long Range Planning Committee has been working diligently and
with independent thought to the overall questions and concerns of the
Fraternity. Samples of those questions are: "How best can we offer Masonry to the younger person?" "How can we effectively streamline our tasks
without losing the original plan of Masonry?" "What should our goals be as
a Fraternity into the twenty-first century?" These are but a few of the primary
issues before this committee. They have produced extensive material for
our Fraternity's consideration. Some of their efforts are recognized in the
very Resolutions now before this Communication. Their task is fraught with
great frustration and one without the constraints that are normal to most
other committee's.
They have extended themselves far beyond what was anticipated. It is
only reasonable to say, 'thank you" for an outstanding job and for the very
extensive and forward thinking material you have lain before us to review,
consider, weigh, digest and possibly adopt over the next few years . Masonry is on the move and this committee has given us a beacon to guide our
Masonic future.

As a Grand Lodge Family for 1990-1991, the twenty-eight officers and
their wives have been privileged to share in one of the greatest experiences
of a Mason's life; an opportunity to spend a great year together, meeting
Masons, experiencing new places and sharing in historic events. Rising at
dawn and driving five hundred miles to Open Grand Lodge or to attend a
reception every night is not the exception. but rather the rule. Getting back
in the car and traveling to the next function, and so on for fifty-two or more
weeks is very tiring but very rewarding. Sharing in each other's personal life
for a year and learning about Masonry in the small as well as the large
communities is a great experience! Missing holidays and anniversaries with
your personal family is a routine of the Grand Lodge Family. This is what
makes the Grand Lodge officers a true family. This is the experience and
the memories of a lifetime!
The support of my Grand Lodge officers this year has been nothing short

of spectacular. The officers were fully dedicated to attend every function
throughout the jurisdiction. Attendance by the appointive line was most
often 100%. Ritual work during Grand Lodge openings and other ritual
events such as cornerstones and dedications were as near perfect in
execution as possible. I thank each and every officer for his total support
and excellence in performance!
Throughounhe year. I have asked the advice of counsel on many issues.
I have talked with many learned Masons and more often than not I have
taken their advice. Sometimes it is best to accommodate the "intent" of the
law rather than the harsh reality of the "literal" law. Above all, I have tried to
consider the hazards of simply "implementing" the law as opposed to first
applying "reasoning" to the final decision. If we are truly "working together"
as a family of Masons, we must be willing to consider all sides of the issues.
Sometimes we must walk beside the path rather than down the "proven" but
very narrow legal path.

great Fraternity. I see us beginning, once again, to believe in our Masonry.

members interested in the Fraternity, if we are to hold them . We must be
willing to accept change to effectively meet the needs of today's society.

him becoming a Mason. We can certainly do that without violating our
obligation. We must now prepare for tomorrow and we must, above all, be
flexible and continue beyond this one year the practice of all of the Bodies
of California Masonry.W orking Together.

DECISION NO. 1
SUSPENSION OF MASTER OF OPPORTUNITY LODGE NO. 740
The Committee on Jurisprude nce:

The Grand Master, acting upon the reports and recommendations of
his Inspector and his Assistant Grand Lecturer, determined that, because of
certain irregularities which had occurred at the Installation of the Master of
Opportunity Lodge in direct contradiction of instructions from the Inspector,
said Master should be suspended pending his cooperation with the Inspector and the Assistant Grand Lecturer. The said Master was suspended but,
thereafter, based upon his agreement to comply with our laws, was restored
to his office.
The Grand Master later learned that, in spite of his promises, said Master
had failed to comply with our law, had attended only two meetings of his
Lodge, and had generally failed to discharge the duties of his office.
Accordingly, the Master was again suspended pending the decision of this
Grand Lodge.
The Grand Master has the power to suspend the Master of any Lodge
from the exercise of the powers and duties of his office, for good cause, until
the next Annual Communication (Section 1016 C.M.C.) and thus the Grand
Master acted wifhin his powers in suspending the Master of Opportuni ty
Lodge No. 740. Your Committee finds that this Decision is consistent with
our law and does not require an amendment to our Code.
As a result, a majority vote only is required for approval. The question
of whether or not such suspension of the Master is to be made permanent
is a matter for this Grand Lodge to decide.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

The first issue here is whether the Grand Master acted properly in
suspending a Master who both refused to conform to established ritual in
conducting his installation, and failed to attend a meeting with the Assistant
Grand Lecturer to discuss that insubordinate conduct, until the Master met
with the Assistant Grand Lecturer and promised to conform to our Code.
Section 1016 of our Code authorizes the Grand Master to suspend a
Master ''for good reasons shown ... " Therefore, the sole question is whether
the Master's recalcitrance constituted good reason. We believe that it
Clearly does. and that the Grand Master's actions were justified.

RECOMMENDATION NO. 1
ELIMINATING PROFICIENCY REQUIREMENT -- THIRD DEGREE
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
The Grand Master has recommended that because there appear to be
no known benefits being realized from requiring a Master Mason to pass a
satisfactory proficiency before applying for membership in a concordant or
appendant organization but that, contrariwise, said requirement has often
been a known deterrent for men interested in joining our Lodges when they
learn of such a proficiency requirement; that the existing requirement of a
Third Degree proficiency as a precondition to joining our concordant or
appendant organizations be eliminated.

Our research regarding the present proficiency requirement of Candidates indicates that the present method does not provide adequate
instruction for, and education of, our Candidates. We agree with the Grand
Master's Recommendation that the best interests of our Fraternity would be
served by reducing the present proficiency requirement. We are of the
opinion that the satisfactory recitation of the obligation and modes of
recognition and the completion of a Basic Masonic Education Course would
be far more effective.
This Committee, therefore, highly recommends the approval of the
Grand Master's Recommendation to shorten the Candidate 's present
proficiency requirement.
Recommendation HELD OVER.
