RECOMMENDATION NO. 3
COST IMPACT OF ADOPTED RESOLUTIONS
The Committee on Jurisprudence:

The Grand Master has recommended that, because often a Resolution
as proposed to our Grand Lodge would, if adopted, result In a substantial
cost impact on the Grand Lodge budget and the annual per capita assessment and without prior knowledge of that impact, the Brethren voting cannot
make a truly sound decision concerning the desirability of the proposed
legislation, all Resolutions should be submitted to the Committee on Finance
for a cost estimate with said estimate being distributed to the Lodges with
the Resolutions themselves.
To carry out the intent of the Grand Master, your Committee on
Jurisprudence submits the following Resolution:
RESOLVED, that sub-section 16th of Section 1008 of the California
Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:
16th. Transmit, at least 150 days prior to the commencement date
of the next Annual Communication, a copy of each and every
Resolution and Recommendation lawfully presented to him,
together with any Recommendations or Decisions made by that
time by the Grand Master, Officers or Committees or Boards of
Grand Lodge, to the members of the Committee on Jurisprudence
for their review and any needed drafting or redrafting as provided
by Section 1204, to transmit at least 90 days prior to the commencement date of the next Annual Communication a copy of each such
Resolution and Recommendation as drafted or redrafted by the
Commjttee on Jurisprudence. to the Committee on Finance for its
review and preparation of an estimate of the cost impact thereof. if
adopted and to transmit at least 60 days prior to the commencement date of the next Annual Communication, a copy of each and
every such Resolution, Recommendation and Decision presented
to him in the form approved by the Committee on Jurisprudence,
together with the brief statement of purpose and effect, as received
from the Committee on Jurisprudence following its review, and the

kost estimates as received from the Committee on Finance. to the
Masters of the several Lodges, Inspectors, and members of the
Committees on Jurisprudence, Policy and General Purposes and

RESOLVED, FURTHER, that Section 1218 of said Code be amended
by adding the following paragraph to follow the first paragraph of said
Section:
Upon receipt from the Grand Secretary of proposed Resolutions
and Recommendations to be considered at the next Annual Communication. the Committee on Finance shall review them and
prepare an estimate of the cost impact of each. if adopted. and
transmit. at least 75 days prior to the commencement date of the
oext Annual Communication, a report of such cost estimates to the
Graod Secretary.
Since this Recommendation seeks to amend the Ordinances, a fivesixths affirmative vote is required for adoption.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

The Grand Master has recommended that Resolutions submitted to
Grand Lodge be referred to the Finance Committee after consideration by
theJurisprud~nce Committee, to address their cost impact on the proposed
budget. The Grand Secretary shall then include this information as part of
the customary data distributed to the Lodges.
We concur with the Grand Master's Recommendation and recommend
a "Yes" vote.
The Committee on Finance:

Your Committee on Finance agrees that the estimated financial impact
of a Resolution is important information and should be conveyed to the
Brethren before the commencement of Grand Lodge when the Resolutions
are sent to the Lodges.
We recommend a "Yes" vote.

RESOLVED, that the California Masonic Code be amen

Sections 501 and 4001 with each said Section to read
as follows:
Written Resolutions, in order to be considered for

proponents.
of at least three members of this Grand Lodge. each
a member of
a different constituent Lodge of this Jurisdiction.
Since this Recommendation seeks to amend our
law. a five-sixths
affirmative vote is required for adoption.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes
hopes that this
proposal will help adequately screen out legislation that
has little or no merit.
Our rules, as they now stand, require that "each and
every" Resolution be
given consideration by Grand Lodge as a whole. Our
state and national
legislative bodies long ago faced this issue of dealin
g with insignificant
legislation by giving broad powers to their committees
. who could effectively
evaluate and, if appropriate, reject legislative propo
sals without taking up
the time of the whose house. We have no such protec
tion in this Grand
Lodge. Every piece of legislation, from the trivial to
the monumental , gets
the same limited consideration. There really needs
to be some test of
relevance before a proponent elects to take up the time
of Grand Lodge by
asking that his proposal be considered . Having to
have the endorsement
of two other Brothers from two other Lodge s might
be a step in the right
direction.

REPORT OF THE GRAND TREASURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:

The Grand Tr~asurer is charged with the responsibility of reporting to
the r:1emb~~s of th~s ~rand Lodge on the financial condition of Grand Lodge
and its ent1t1es, which include the Masonic Homes of California, the California
Masonic Memorial Temple and the California Masonic Foundation. The
~o~ti~ui~g financial contributions to these entities by the members of this
1unsd1ct1on have been very generous. Your support makes it all possible.
Thank you.
The reports and comments of the Grand Treasurer are based on the
official statements of Deloitte and Touche, Certified Public Accountants of
San Francisco, whose reports are an integral part of the Grand Treasurer's
Report. Their audit covers the year ending June 30, 1991, and contains a
complete record of income and expenses for the period.
The delegates to the Annual Communication, are in effect, the stockholders of the entities of Grand Lodge and you are encouraged, and it is
rec om mended, that you read and review this report. Your observations and
comments are appreciated .
While certain governments may operate with fiscal deficits. that is not
the pro~ince of your Grand Lodge. Prudence in managing the assets and
controlling the expenses of Grand Lodge and its entities is of the highest
p~iority. Fiscal responsibility is the cornerstone of Freemasonry in California. Rest assured, that the assets and investments of our Masonic entities
are well managed and protected in a manner of which you can be justifiably
proud.
During the past year, a new firm of accountants was engaged, Deloitte
and Touche of San Francisco. With their assistance and the complete
support and cooperation of our Masonic entities, especially our Masonic
Hon:ies B~ard of Trustees, an entirely new management information system
for financial acco~nting and related functions was installed. This change
was made to provide the members of this jurisdiction with the most accurate
and timely financial information possible.

Our special thanks to the Most Worshipful Ronald A. Sherod and his
team of Grand Lodge Officers for their strong support and cooperation this
past year. To our retiring Grand Secretary, our deepest gratitude for his
wisdom, guidance and counsel. Particular recognition is hereby noted to
our Accounting Staff under the direction of Nurys Erazo. Thank you, one
and all, for your dedication ard diligence. Through your sincere personal
effort, our new management information system reached fruition of target.
Respectfully submitted,
H. Herbert P. Wilkins, Grand Treasurer

ACTION BY GRAND LODGE

The Committee on Charters
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
Most Worshipful Grand Master, Distinguished Guests and Brethren, on
behalf of the Charters Committee I am pleased to report that we chartered
Fox-Coates Daylight Lodge No. 842 on November 10, 1990. They hold their
Stated Meetings on the Second Tuesday morning of each month in the
Victorville Masonic Temple at Victorville, California. We have no Masonic
Clubs working at this time, nor do we have any Lodges under dispensation.
This year we have had fifteen two Lodge consolidations and three three
Lodge consolidations. We now have five hundred and six chartered Blue
Lodges in our jurisdiction.
That portion of the Grand Secretary's Report dealing with changes of
meeting place of Lodges under Sections 2098 and 2100 of the California
Masonic Code and the consolidation of Lodges under Section 2104 of the
California Masonic Code. have been referred to this Committee for consideration. We find that all of the requirements of our laws have been
complied with and .recommend that the Grand Secretary be authorized to
property endorse the charters of those Lodges. A listing of those Lodges is
included in a part of the Grand Secretary's Report.
On behalf of the Charters Committee, we thank you for the privilege and
honor of serving you and our Fraternity this year.

The microfilm system consists of a Minolta high speed filmer and an
RP504M viewer/printer.
When the filming of the historical records for both members and Lodges
is completed. it is proposed to then extend this service to the California
Masonic Homes records and the other parts of our office. We will, when
completed, be in possession of a complete back-up copy of all records
which can be stored off-site for safety. We also will have some extra floor
space available to us, of which we are rapidly running out.

NEW EDITION - CALIFORNIA MASONIC CODE
In 1988, Grand Master Leo B. Mark, recommended at the Annual
Communication, that a Committee be appointed by the incoming Grand
Master to rewrite the then existing Code using simple every day layman's
language.
That Committee was formed and has worked long and hard throughout
the last three years to accomplish its assigned task. At this Annual Communication we have the result of their labors. The cost for the new Code
will be the same as that of the old Code, $15.00 each.
The new Code has been completely re-written, re-structured and renumbered from front to back. It will be in a loose-leaf format . Annotations
which are relevant have been included in the body of the Section itself and
all Annotations, as such, have been deleted from the book.
The language, as set forth in the Code, is simple and understardable.
But the greatest achievement is the index. This has to be the crowning jewel
of the Committee's work. It is complete and in some cases, overly so; each
entry is clear and has a brief description of the Section itself. This Code is
a fine example of the talents and the diligence of the members of this Grand
Jurisdiction.
CONCLUSION
As I conclude my eleventh and final report to the Grand Lodge, I would
be remiss if I did not express my great appreciation to all those dedicated
Masons who serve this Grand Lodge because of their love for our Fraternity.
Over the course of these past eleven years, it has been my extreme
good fortune to have been permitted to work and to socialize with hundreds
of truly fine men and their ladies, not only from within our jurisdiction, but

TRIAL RECORD NO. 2142
Your Committee has considered the Petition for Restoration in Trial
Record No. 2142. Your Committee believes that the evidence indicates this
former member of Table Mountain Lodge No. 124 has shown sufficient
realization of the circumstances leading to his expulsion. This is evidenced
by his change of outlook, his rehabilitation, and acceptance of him ~y his
Lodge and community. Sufficient time has elapsed since the expulsion to
Indicate that these positive factors are not temporary changes.

ACTION BY GRAND LODGE
TRIAL RECORD NO. 2173

The Committee on Trial Review:
There have been referred to your Committee on Trial Review, since the
1990 Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge, eighteen (18) Trials, of
which three (3) are Applications for Restoration.
Your Committee has reviewed each of the Trial Records numbered
2316,2320,2321,23 23,2324, 2325,2326,2327,23 29,2329a,and2331 ,and
finds that in each case there was substantial compliance with the procedural
requirements of our Constitution and Ordinances, and the result is supported by the evidence in the records of each case and that there are no
miscarriages of justice.

In Trial Record No. 2173 , a former member of Malta Lodge No. 588 (now
known as Malta El Sereno No. 588) was charged with a violation of California
Penal Code No. 647a, in that he molested his step-daughter. a child under
the age of 18 years. He entered a plea of "Not Guilty" and a jury trial was
held on May 18, 1978, in which he was found "Guilty ." One of the conditions
of his sentence was that he register pursuant to California Penal Code
Section 290 as a "sex offender."

Your Committee.therefore submits the following Resolution:

After the conviction and sentence, which was affirmed on appeal,
charges of unmasonic conduct were filed on October 21, 1978. He was
found "Guilty" of unmasonic conduct and the penalty was fixed at Expulsion.
This was affirmed by Grand Lodge in October, 1982.

RESOLVED. that in each of the above numbered Trial Records. the
judgment and penalty imposed be and are ratified , affirmed and
approved .

He has applied for resto ration on three previous occasions: September
23, 1987, June 5, 1989, May 14, 1990 and these three applications were
denied on October 12, 1988, October 9, 1989 and October 8, 1990 by Grand
Lodge.

Resolution ADOPTED.
He again seeks restoration and has offered letters of personal reference
and recommendations, but has not submitted any independent evidence of
remorse and rehabilitation as suggest ed t o him in a letter from Grand Lodge
on October 16, 1990. Again, his request does not express any remor~e or
rehabilitation. He has not presented any evidence that he is still not required

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

to be registered as a sex offender for his criminal conviction. We believe
that the petitioner fails to understand the crime of which he was convicted
and for which he was expelled. At the Stated Meeting held on July 2, 1991.
the Lodge recommended restoration.

102

The violation is so severe that your Committee feels that clear, unequivocal, independent evidence of remorse and rehabilitation must be given
before your Committee can recommend any action except that the petition
be again denied.
We therefore submit the following Resolution:
RESOLVED, that the petition for Restoration in Trial Record No.
2173 be denied.

Report ADOPTED.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 2292
In Trial Record No. 2292, a member of Temescal Lodge No. 314 pied
"Guilty'' in Superior Court to embezzling more than $150,000 from his
employer, the Municipality of Fontana, California. In 1988, this conviction
gave rise to the filing of charges of unmasonic conduct and the Trial Master
found the member "Guilty" and set the penalty at Suspension. Because of
the seriousness of the crime the Grand Lodge increased the penalty to
Expulsion in October. 1989. The member has now petitioned for restoration
and provided letters from his present employer and others.
A letter of support for restoration was signed by 39 Masons who
acknowledge they were not aware of the facts of the charges. Pursuant to
California Masonic Code Section 2516, a vote of the Lodge was taken at a
Stated Meeting and 12 of 18 members voted to oppose this member's
restoration.
In view of the serious nature of the offense, the amount involved, the
vote of his Lodge and the brevity of time since expulsion, your Committee
submits the following Resolution:
RESOLVED, that the Petition for Restoration in Trial Record No.
2292 be denied.

Report ADOPTED.

Real £state Report
by Gerald A. Sharer, Chairman

Our Homes Representatives, along with Lodge Comm
ittees, interview
our applicants for admission to the Homes and those
for Nonresident
Assistance.

The Real Estate Committee of the Masonic Homes of
California consists
of Gerald A Sharer, Eugene R. Perkins and Vert Lobb.

MEETINGS

The function of the Committee is to dispose of Real
Estate made
available to the Masonic Homes by residents, gifts
and wills and other
bequests.

Meetings of the Trustees are usually held on the first
Wednesday of the
month, alternating between the Union City and Covin
a Homes.
The meetings are frequently attended by the Chairm
an of the Homes
Endowment Board, as well as some of the Endowment
Board members.
Many Committee meetings are held on the Tuesd
ay afternoon or
evening preceding the regular meeting. Most of the Comm
ittee Reports are
prepared in advance for distribution at or prior to the
regular meeting.
You will note that the Administrators and members
of the Board of
Trustees have been given the opportunity to participate
in the preparation
of this Annual Report as follows:

at the Union City
Home and in the South at the Children's Home in Covin
a. The Admissions
Committee has Co-Chairmen. Currently, Alvin J . Weis
serves as Chairman
in the North and Verl Lobb as Chairman in the South
. They are supported
by six other members of the Board of Trustees; three each
from the Northern
and Southern part of the State. The considered recom
mendations of the
full Committee are presented by the Chairmen to the
Board for their approval. The Co-Chairmen are responsible to make the
necessary coord ination with the Masonic Homes Representative, the Admin
istrators of Union

has generated
$3, 126,762.00 income for the General Fund .

notes are secured by

Treasurer's Report
by Henry P. Wilkins, Treasurer

Each and every year for nearly a century, Californ ia Masons have been
asked to aid and support the Masonic Homes of California. You have never
failed in your obligation to the thousands of Masons. widows and orphans
who have enjoyed the benefits of your largesse.
As we head into the 21st Century, the needs of our Homes grows ever
larger. The average age of our Fraternity is mute evidence of this
phenomenon. The sheer costs of maintaining our properties is elephantine.
The ravages of inflation have been particularly hard on maintaining our
Homes.
Fiscal prudence has become the touchstone of the Masonic Homes
the
Board of Trustees. The dedication of the Board Members to maintaining

It has been a distinct pleasure for the Grand Treasurer. in unity with the
Board of Trustees of the Homes and the entire membership of this jurisdiction, to carry out our solemn obligation to those whom we have given our
pledge -- to care for those in need.
What better evidence to our commitment is there than our two beautiful
the

Publicity Committee Report
by Ver/ Lobb, Chairman

The Publicity Committee of the Board of Trustees during the past year
has completed numerous articles for the California Freemason. The purpose of these articles is to keep the Fraternity informed of the good work
they are doing through their support of the Masonic Homes. These articles
contain personal stories of Brothers, wives, widows and children who have
had their lives changed and improved by living in the Masonic Homes.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

REPORT OF THE ADMINISTRATOR

embrace the Covina community and it's adjacent areas utilizing common
resources.

MASONIC HOMES, COVINA

1990-1991
THE EVOLUTION AT COVINA
This past year has been one of growth; growth not only in population
but in the quality of service and the manner in which service is delivered.
Covina's growth is unusual in that the children's program has stabilized
at an average of 28 residents and the adult program is growing along
predicted trends.
Portions of our programs at Covina are jointly allocated such as administration, dietary and facUity maintenance. Where one program seems
more cost efficient due to a higher population, the other gives the opposite
impression.
Your Board of Trustees carefully watches not only expenditures but is
fully dedicated in ensuring that each resident, regardless of age, has a safe,
secure and dignified life in a quality environment. This includes fine housing,
good nutrition, activities conducive to each resident's needs and desires,
and effective health care.
THE COVINA ADULT PROGRAM
This has been our first full fiscal year of operation with both child and
adult care programs adjacent one another. We have completed the planned
expansion and our goal to fill a greater need has come to fruition.
Voluntary relationships have formed between many of our children and
adult residents and has the predicted affect of multiplying the benefit to both.
On January 8, 1990, the adult program at Covina commenced its
operations. Our population has grown to 30 ambulatory residents. We
project growth to 40 adult residents in 28 apartments during the next fiscal
year. The elderly in need and approved for admission will continue to be
admitted to the Adult Home at Covina and the population will ultimately
stabilize at between 75 to 85 residents.
The adults living at Covina have available a variety of recreational,
education and spiritual activities of interest to senior citizens. Our residents

153

Although Covina is not a licensed health care facility, the Masonic Home
health care program has been enhanced to provide assistance to aging
persons who need extra care to remain suitably and happily placed at
Covina for as long as possible with the provision of excellent health care for
all. Our residents have access to programs relating to their own health
maintenance.
THE COVINA CHILD CARE PROGRAM
We are proud to announce the employment of Brother Ronald C. Bunte
(334) as Director of Children's Services. After 31 years of experience in the
public school arena, he brings to the Masonic Home a fresh insight into the
chUd care program. Brother Ron is supervised by the Administrator and has
concentrated on a more formal preparation of children for independent
living, enhancement of the role of the Houseparent as the primary level of
care, improving the children's academic program, and improving contact
with guardians, Lodges and extended family members through various
media.
We continue to assure that children receive educational assistance. The
Masonic Home utilizes non-certificated proctors for specific subject assistance and a certificated tutor for 1: 1 tutoring of our elementary students. At
the elementary age the basic foundations of study are learned.
Through the Director of Children's Services, Houseparents provide
effective supervision for residents while on planned activities, regardless of
the activity location. Support services are available to the Houseparents to
assure that they have time to dedicate themselves to each child. Our
Houseparents are residential employees and live in the cottage with the
chDdren they serve. No resident is alone and without supervision whDe in
the cottage.
The Masonic Home has developed guidelines for the discipline of
chBdren. Discipline Is learning and the Masonic Home favors the concept
of using "natural and logical consequences" and teaches discipline as "skills
that show caring." Natural consequences are things that happen as a result
of the initial action. Logical consequences closely link the consequence to
the type of inappropriate behavior.
Activities are well rounded and include educational, spiritual and recreational programs benefiting residents. Mature and responsible residents may

engage in supervised off-grounds activities without Houseparent supervision, i.e., dates, picnics, beach trips, theater, etc. The Houseparent
assigned to a cottage has primary responsibility for determining the level of
maturity and responsibility of the resident requesting this privilege.

CURRENT TRENDS
The Masonic Home has completed a study and computerization of our
alumni information. We have an association which has become more active
and which meets annually. Basic information is maintained which permits
continued contact with alumni In order to assist them if possible.
In our 91 year history we have touched the lives of 1,372 children. Prior
to my employment date of June 1, 1981, the average age upon admission
of a child was 9.8 years and the average length of residency was 5.4 years.
During the last ten years the average age upon admission has been 10.6
years and the average length of stay 3.2 years. It is obvious that we are
receiving children at an older age and, when appropriate, assisting them in
returning to a family which has been re-unified.
Older children who are placed outside the family often have preconceived impulses and persuasions which are more difficult to improve.
Despite our difficult tasks, your Masonic Home continues to do excellent
work consistent with the will of God and our obligations as Masons.
For children remaining through adulthood, the Masonic Homes of
California continues it's caring through a scholarship program administered
by the Administrator and supervised by the Scholarship Committee of the
Board of Trustees. Applications are submitted for higher education in
accredited colleges and universities or vocational schools approved by the
Scholarship Committee.

As directed by the Grand Master, your committee has met with a similar
committee of P.rince Hall Mas?ns (on May 18 and June 15). These meetings
have been serious and cordial , and we sincerely believe they have been
productive for both committees . These meetings occurred only after concurrence through each Grand Lodge's office.

Recently a number of Grand Lodges have acted to recognize the Prince
Hall Grand Lodge in their respective jurisdictions. They are --. Colorado,
Connecticut , Idaho, Minnesota, Nebraska, North Dakota. Washington and
Wisconsin. These actions took place in 1989, 1990 and 1991. Although the
terms of recognition vary from one Grand Lodge to another, there appears
to be a course toward changing attitudes. This development should not be
overlooked.

To summarize our activities. your committee was formed on October
29, 1990, and commenced researching readily available written information

about Prince ~all Masonry. On December 8 an organizational meeting was
~eld at Seafaring Lodge No. 708 in Newport Beach. This meeting resulted
in our December 16 letter to the Grand Secretary requesting the respective
Grand .Masters to me~t informally. On February 16, 1991, a meeting of your
committee was held in San Diego. This meeting was timed to take place
during the Annual Conference of the Grand Masters of North America. The
timing and location allowed members of your committee to personally meet
and talk to people we had contacted in those Grand Lodges who have
previou~ly stu.died '.~ince Hall recognition. Each contact person had played
a ~art 1.n th~1r off1c1al process of recognition. Having been given the
California Prince Hall Committee Chairman's name, numerous phone calls
and. f~~e-to-fa~e m~e~i~gs occurred between the Chairmen in establishing
the in1t1al and h1stonc 101nt committee meeting on May 18, 1991, in Oakland.
At this initial meeting the background of Resolution No. 90-7 was reviewed.
A short history of Prince Hall Masonry in California was presented. Following
several ph.one calls and meetings between the Chairmen, a second meeting
was held in Oakland on June 15. Representatives of the MW Prince Hall
Grand Lodge of California verbally indicated their desire for some form of
official recognition. A public or lodge information process was described
as needed to handle any fears, apprehension, misunderstanding or concerns so that the expectations of each Grand Lodge could be addressed.
At its July 20 meeting the Special Committee met to develop the initial draft
version of the committee report. At the August 24 meeting this final report
was completed.
Obviously, your committee has no knowledge of the rituals of the Prince
Hall Grand Lodge or of the quality of their ritual work. However, we are
impressed with the quality of the Prince Hall men we have met. There can
be no question about their sincerity, their seriousness, their high moral
standards. their devotion to their fraternity; in short, we are convinced that
Prince Hall Masons are men of very fine character. Because of these
cont~cts. ~he ~ommittee is convinced that this is the time to develop a firm
relat1onsh1p with the MW Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California. Inc.

163

Your committee has gathered a vast amount of written material involving
history, current policy and law, interpretatio~ of applic.able ~ublic law, e~c.
All of this requires meticulous review and serious considera.t1on. O~ special
significance are (1) the history of Prince Hall Freemasonrx in Americ~, and
(2) interpretation and application of the so-called American Doctrine of
Exclusive Territorial Jurisdiction.
Implementation of Grand Master Sherod's "Mission Statement" to your
special study committee clearly requires thoughtful, ca.reful and thorough
deliberation , a process that certainly must not be done in haste.
We believe we are progressing properly and that appropriate recommendations can and will be developed for possible resolution at the 1992
Annual Communication of our Grand Lodge.
We believe our Prince Hall counterparts feel as we do about the
important need •tor thoughtful progression toward enhancing our future
relationships.
In conclusion, our committee recommends that it be con~i~ued for the
1991/92 Masonic year, as presently composed, with the explicit charge to
bring before the 1992 Annual Communication its proposals ?nd recommen -

dations respecting some form of recognition of the MW Prince Hall Grand
Lodge of California, Inc. and als~ that the Gr~nd Master, ~he Deputy Gr~nd
Master and their designees continue to meet informally wit~ co~responding
representatives of the MW Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California, Inc.

Your committee wishes to thank the Grand Lodge for allowing it to serve
and it hopes that its efforts will meet with the approv~I of Grand .~odge. We
wish to thank the Grand Master for this confidence m us. Add1t1on~lly, w_e
wish to thank the proponent of Resolution No. 90-7 for suggesting this
important and timely study.

ADVERTISING IN EAST-WEST
FOOTBALL GAME PROGRAM
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

Your Committee on Polic y and General Purposes, in recent years, has
been opposed to relaxing the restrictions of the California Masonic Code as
it relates to paid advertisements in Trestleboards and bulletins and other
publications of Masonic related organizations without adequate controls to
prevent abuses. This year's Committee is of the same opinion.
There is no question of the great work being done by the Shrine in their
Hospitals for Crippled Children and the Burn Institutes. The Shrine is to be
commended for this success.

Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

It is the opinion of this Committee that all Masons and Masonic Organizations in this jurisdiction should be treated equally. Whenever special
interest laws are passed. those laws give one group of members privileges
that are not shared by other groups. This is not in keeping with the long
standing policy of this Grand Lodge.
The Grand Master pointed out that it is unfortunate that the advertising
which is in violation of Masonic Code has gone unchecked. That prohibition
is still in effect and the practice should be curtailed.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No"
vote.
Recommendation NOT APPROVED.

With regard to the termination of dispensation
for a Lodge, California
Masonic Code Section 2018 clearly calls for the
termination to take effect
on Octo ber 1st thus rendering a Lodge U.O., to
be non-existent durin g the
time of the Annual Communication of Grand Lodg
e, and its members who
do not hold dual or plural membership are releg
ated to the status of
non-affiliated Master Masons in good standing
(assuming no unmasonic
cond uct charges exist or are pending). This actio
n would cause a member
with non-affiliated Master Mason status to be inelig
ible to attend the Grand
Lodge Annual Communication under California Maso
nic Code Section 158.
Your Committee concurs that the law should be
changed to allow members
in good standing to attend Grand Lodg e.
However, point number 2 covering the right of a
Lodge U.O. to vote at
the Grand Lodge Annual Communication cause
s us some conc ern. A
dispensation is issued to a new Lodge as a trial
period during which time
said Lodge shall demonstrate qualification, provi
de necessary certificates
of proficiency, be clear of all indebtedness and exhib
it satisfactory evidence
of its Masonic capability before becoming a duly
chartered Lodge. Until
such time as Grand Lodge approves the issuing of
a charter to a Lodge U.D.,
that Lodge is considered a probationary Lodge, not
a duly chartered Lodge,
and therefore should not be entitled to vote in Gran
d Lodge until a charter
is issued.

Your Committee on Policy and General Purpo
ses recognizes that we
are having problems in the acquisttion and reten
tion of candidates. We
conc ede that our present proficiency requireme
nts proba bly contribute, in
some degre e. to these problems. And we certa
inly agree there is a great
need to improve our progr ams for candidate educ
ation . However, there are
a numb er of other factors which contribute to our
difficulties in getting the
retaining candidates and we are not convinced
that the virtual elimination of
the profic iency requirements would have any positi
ve impa ct towar d solving
these probl ems.

require the candidate to

ing.

We are also conc erned that adoption of this Reso
lution in its present
form would incor porat e the proposed questions
into the Masonic Code.
This means that revision or elimination of these
questions, or the addition of
new ones . could only be accomplished by a 5/6th
s vote of Grand Lodg e.
Finally, the candidate 's proficiencies are a part
of the adop ted ritual of
the Grand Lodg e and cann ot be altered or delet
ed unless Section 2690 of
the California Maso nic Code is revised or delet
ed. This Section provides
that "Grand Lodge alone has the power to chan
ge ritual for the purpo se of
having it remain as it was handed down from time
immemorial."
We cann ot ignore the restriction of this section
. For all of the reasons
stated, we must recommend a "No" vote.
The Committee on Ritual:
The Ritual Committee supports the conc ept of a
shortened candidate' s
profic iency. We demo nstrated our posttion when
we endorsed Resolution
90-26 , both last year and this.
Resolution 91-1, while providing a shorter profic
iency , merely exchanges one set of memorized questions and answ
ers for another set . It sill
does not effectively acco mmo date the limited time
a potential candidate is
willing to spend . Can we really afford to conti nue
to waste time experimenting with half-way measures?
We hope you recog nize that this resol ution
would require every
candidates' coach in California to forget everything
he knows and learn new
questions and answers before he could continue
coaching. I wond er how
many of our long-time coaches would be willin
g to continue unde r those
circumstances.

The Committee on Ritual must recommend a "No"

and may be both pleased and proud to

We oppose this change for a second reas
on as well. We are not at all
sure that the language which the prop
onents seek to change is part of the
ritual. However, that is how the proponen
ts have characterized it. If they
are correct, existing law would not perm
it the proposed change in the ritual.
Section 2690 of our law restricts the pow
er of the grand Lodge to change
our ritual to those alterations which are
implemented ''for the purpose of
having it remain as it was handed dow
n from time immemorial." Thus our
law allows corrections in the ritual to resto
re it to the way it was originally,
but does not allow innovations which requ
ire the ritual to be given in a way
which has never been don e before.
The proponents do not contend that
the prop osed change would
restore the current ritual to the manner
in which it was delivered in 'time
immemorial." Unless the proposed chan
ge is a correction, rather than an
innovation, it is contrary to the policy of
this Grand Lodge, as memorialized
in Section 2690.
For both of these reasons, your Com
mittee on Polic y and General
Purposes recommends a "No" vote on
Resolution 91 -8.
The Com mittee on Ritual:

You consid ered this same Resolution last
year and it received only 445
"Yes" votes, less than 29%. Frankly, we
are surp rised to see it again so soon.
Our opposition to this Resolution was
clearly stated at the 1990 Communication, and we repeat it now. "The
authors of this Resolution corr ectly
state that non-citizens should not be expe
cted to Pledge their Allegianc e to
a flag other than their own. We would hope
that all such persons wou ld have
presence of mind enough to realize
that they were exempted from the
Master's directive as now stated in our
Monitor. Considering the frequency
with which our Pledge is recited, they
should be well acquainted with
behavior appropriate to their status.
While we are sympathetic to the inten
t of the authors, we feel this
legislation is unnecessary, and recomme
nd a "No" vote.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This Resolution would permit the wearing of a Past Master's apron while
occupying an officer's chair on Past Master's Night. This comminee can
find no legitimate, or acceptable reason for anyone occupying any officer
chair not to wear the jewel and apron appropriate to that chair. Since this
Resolution is limited only to one night of the year, and that presumably only
Past Masters will be occupying the officer's chairs and will be recognized
as Past Masters. the wearing of any apron other than that of the station
should not be permined.
We urge a "No" vote.

The Committee on Ritual:
As we travel throughout this Jurisdiction, we see an amazing variety of
officers' aprons, ranging form beautifully embroidered. ornate aprons for
each office. down to simple, plain white aprons. Obviously, it is the jewel ,
not the apron, which identifies the office. Therefore. we see no problem in
allowing Past Masters to wear their aprons while serving as officers during
special Past Masters' nights.
We remind the brethren that this Resolution permits the wearing of that
apron only "on the occasion of a Lodge' s Past Master's Night. " In other
enjoy the same privilege. Our law will still
words, when all participants
prohibit the wearing of a Past Master's apron while filling an office on any
other occasion, and that restriction should be rigorously enforced.

w~I

With that understanding, the Committee on Ritual recommends a "Yes"
vote.

The Committee on Juri spru den ce:
The proponents of Resolution No 91-1
3 seek to establish a committee.
with a fixed three year life, to review exis
ting Grand Lodge committees. and
present legislaton to reduce, eliminate
or consolidate those with over\apping
or unnecessary functions and, also ,
to prevent the formation of any new
committees without a two thirds vote
in Grand Lodge.
The legislation as distributed to the Con
stituent Lodges is adequate to
carry out the intent of the proponents.

This Resolution seeks to amend our

law and a 5/6 affirmative vote is

required for adoption.
The Committee on Policy and General

Purposes :
Study of Existing Committees and
Limitation On Creation of New
Special Committees .
The subiect of appointing Study Com
mittees to explore the entire
committee structure of our Grand Lod
ge has been an ongoing concern of
this Grand Lodge in recent years. In
reviewing this subject in prior Annual
Proceedings . we note that two such stud
y committees have been appointed
during this period .
Most Worshipful Donald G. Ingalls, at
the recommendation of the 1978
Policy and General Purposes Committe
e. appointed a blue-ribbon commission to carefully examine the organiza
tional structure of the Grand Lodge of
California, and also that of other Gran
d jurisdictions; it was charged to
formally report the results of its study
and its conclusions at the next annual
communication. This commission mad
e its report to the Grand Lodge in
1981 after an extensive two-year stud
y.
In 1986. Grand Master John W. Dris
kell's recommendation number 3
again addressed this subject and sugg
ested that the incoming Grand Master
appoint a special study commission
to explore the entire committee structure of this Grand Lodge and if foun
d necessary. to make appropriate
recommendations to the Grand Master
tor his consideration or the submission of legislation on a timely basis
to be considered at the next annual
communication. Such committee was
appointed and continued its in-depth
study tor the next two years. The resu
lts of its findings are recorded in the
1988 Proceedings.
Grand Masters currently have the auth
ority and have recently exercised
it by consolidating and restricting com
mittees as deemed necessary.

Robert,H. Balderree, PM No. 561

The third "whereas" statement of this Resolution
sets out some of the
reasons that previous similar Resolutions presented
to Grand Lodge have
not been recommended by the Committee on Polic
y and General Purposes
for adoption.
A Resolution to change a fundamental, democratic
provision of our
Constitution, which has functioned well for many years
, should demonstrate
a need more important than the mere possibility of
increased attendance at
our Annual Communications .
Credential Committee reports in recent years
have shown that approximately one-quarter to one-third of the regist
ered attendees at the
Annual Communication are Past Masters. Only
a part of these can vote.
If this Resolution were adopted to allow four votes
to Past Masters of
each Lodge, they could, if they wished. override the
total votes of the current
Master, Wardens and Elective Respresentative .
Confusion within Lodges
could be invited.
Because of the proportionately heavier load on
their memberships.
many of the smaller or outlying Lodges could
neither help finance nor
physically furnish three additional Past Masters who
would be able to attend
the Communications .
We believe our long establish provisions that each
Lodge be allowed
the reasonable opportunity to be equally repre
sented in Grand Loclge
should be continued .
A Lodge whose membership is small , or at a consi
derable distance from
San Francisco. should continue to nave the same
size of democratic voice
through its elective officers as a larger Lodge, or
one closer to San Francisco.

This Resolution seeks to amend our law and a

5/6 affirmative vote is

required for adoption.
The Committee on Polic y and General Purp oses:

This Resolution would chan ge our law in three distin
ct ways. First of all ,
it would prevent the Grand Maste r from maki
ng any recommendations
during the last 180 days before Grand Lodge.
Second , it would limit the
length of each committee report concerning a Reso
lution to the same time
limits imposed upon a member speaking from
the floor. Third . it would
prohibit committees in general, and Policy and Gene
ral Purposes
Committee in particular, from making any recom

R

mendation concerning
the passage of a Resolution . We oppose each chan
ge.

'?

There is good reason why the Grand Master
is exempted from the
normal requirement that any Resolution must
be subm itted 180 days in
advance of the annual communication. During this
extensive travels around
the jurisdiction, and throu gh his day-to-day incolv
ement in the operation of
the Grand Lodge, a Grand Master becomes aware
of pro blems. and potential solutions to problems, in a way to a d egree which
the rest of the Fraternity
does not. He .is exempted from the 180-day limit
so that he can present
those ideas to the Grand Lodge for its prompt consi
deration, even though
those problems or solutions may not have come
to his attent ion until the
second six months of his term. We do not think that
the potential for a hasty

those "late" rec omm endations should be prohibited .

Turning to the secon d proposal--that of limiting the
length of comm ittee
reports--we note that all the recitals of the Resolution
are directed solely to
the first proposal. Nowhere does the proponent
explain why limits should
be placed on the length of a comm ittee's report.
Nevertheless. it is not hard to understand the reaso
ning behing this pa rt
of the Resolution . We understand, and we share
in, the frustration that the
delegates feel when a committee report concerning
a Resolution is three or
four minutes in length, and yet the proponent
of that Resolution has his
microphone cut off alter two minutes. And since
this committee reports on
every Resolution . we are not surprised that a good
deal of that frustration is
directed at us.

234

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

We submit to you, however, that such frustration is misdir
ected . What
is the source of this inequity? The problem is not that
committee reports
are too long, but that the opportunity to speak from
the floor is too short.
The solution, therefore, is not to reduce the length of the
committee reports,
but to eliminate the arbitrary restrictions on the length
of floor debate by
delegates.

PROVIDES FOR ALL COMMITTEE REPORTS ON

Finally , the third aspect of the Resolution seeks to preve
nt any committee from voicing support for or opposition to the pendi
ng Resolution. Once
again, no reason for this radical change is offered by
the proponent, and we
can find none ourselves. We feel that there are good
reasons why each
committee which reports, whether it be Finance, Ritual
, Policy and General
Purposes, or some other committee to which the
proposal has been
referred, should be allowed to advise the delegates
of that committee's
evaluation of the merits of the proposal.
After all, it is you. the members of Grand Lodge , who
decide what the
decisions and policies of the Grand Lodge shall be,
not the committees.
Legislative proposals are referred to those committees
only because the
committees are expected to have some degree of exper
tise in the subject.
The committees then report to you so that your vote
can be based on the
most complete and most authoritative information availa
ble.
This restriction is poorly advised as to the report of any
committee, but
especially those of Policy and General Purposes. This
committee exists for
the sole purpose of evaluating and reporting on legisla
tive proposals. Our
very function is to say whether, in our opinion, a
particualr proposal is
consistant with the policy and direction of the Grand
Lodge ; in short, our
pupos e is to advise Grand Lodge . There is no way
that we can fulUI that
purpose, unless we include that advice--that is, our recom
mendation --in our
report. Our entire report is a recommendation, togeth
er with an explanation
of the reasons behind it. If we are to be prohibited
from delivering that
advice, what function does the proponent envision
that this committee
would fulfill?
Because each of the three parts of this Resolution
is contrary to the
sound policy of the Grand Lodge, your Committee on
Policy and General
Purposes recommends a "No" vote on Resolution 91-25
.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

Many other committees to whom proposed legislation is referred mett
during the Annual Communication and separate meetings prior thereto
should not be necessary.
In order that copies of their reports could be circulated to the membership at least 60 days prior to the Communication, as required by this
Resolution, it is obvious that committees to whom Resolutions are referred
would have to hold meetings prior to that 60 day limit. This would result in
unnecessary added expense to the Grand Lodge and could deter
proponents from meeting with committees unless they were able to be
present at the designated time of such meetings. Withour hearing
proponents statements, a committee might not make accurate recommendations in all situations.
We believe that the best interests of the proponents of amendments. as
well as those of the delegates to Grand Lodge, are best served by the manner
in which proposed legislation is handled presently.
Your Committee recommends a "No" vote.
The Committee on Finance:

The Finance Committee does not believe that the results of this
proposed Resoltuion will enhance the discussions of the speakers on the
Resolutions during the Annual Communications and therefoe the additional
costs of the additional meetings required to comply with the proposed
Resolution, which are estimeated at a minimum of $5,000.00 , are not
justified. Therefore, your Committee on Finance recommends a "No" vote.

(91-29)

WHEREAS, it is desirable that all persons becoming members of the
Masonic Fraternity develop an early appreciation of the nature and stature
of our organization ; and
WHEREAS, nothing transpires at a Stated Meeting which is unfit or
Improper for the ears of an Entered Apprentice or Fellowcraft Mason; and
WHEREAS, an often lengthy period of time passes between a
candidate's initiation, and through no fault of his own, his obtaining the
sublime degree of Master Mason; and
WHEREAS, the present practice of holding all Stated Meetings in the
Third Degree prevents Entered Apprentice and Fellowcraft Masons from
observing and studying the inner workings of a Masonic Lodge, though such
study and observation would be beneficial to their Masonic education in
regard to the California Masonic Code and the charitable work we strive to
achieve; and
WHEREAS, it is desirable to permit immediate involvement by Initiates.
which would be beneficial to the Lodge by faster advancement of the
candidates through the degrees.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that the second sentence of
Section 2034 of the California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:
All business, except the examination of applicants and the conferring of the first aAd second and third degrees. shall be done in a
Lodge of Entered Apprentice Ma64ef Masons. Only Master Masons
shall be eligible to vote.

WHEREAS, Grand Lodge has for years been offering workshops,
retreats and other programs emphasizing leadership and effective Lodge
management as being essential to the future of every Masonic Lodge; and
WHEREAS, the Committee on the Conference of Younger Members

on leading the Lodge and planning its programs; and

of the Masons of California responded that their Lodge anendance would
subst~ntially _increase if Lodge leadership was more effective, providing
more interesting and meaningful meetings; and
. WHEREAS, 40% of the Masons surveyed (above) indicated their interest in Lodge activities would almost certainly increase if their leadership skills
could be more effectively developed within the Lodge ; and

W~EREAS, over two-thirds of the non-Masons surveyed by the
Ma~onic Renewal Task Force wish to develop their leadership skills and 51 %
desire to take a leadership role; and

for Lodge officers, resultmg in an imbalance between ritual and management

There has long been a concern that preparation for Lodge leadership has
been almost exclusively in the area of ritual, and little or no training has been
done insofar as proper conduct of meeting, program planning that will
contribute to members' interest, appointment and supervision of committees, budgetary and fiscal matters, interpersonal relationships, and the
whole host of problems related to the leadership of a Lodge of Master
Masons.
Yet, when there has been a breakdown of leadership, when we have a
disfunctional Master, it has been extremely rare that it has resulted from the
lack of ritual preparation. It has almost always resulted from a faWure to
provide the Lodge with adequate leadership.
Without diminishing our concern for ritual proficiency, it is time that we
give some official recognition to the importance of Lodge management. Will
this insure that every Master is going to have great and stimulating Lodge

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Membership in our Lodges is open to all men who believe in a Supreme
Being and a future existence, are of good moral c onduct, and have no
physical or mental impairment which would prevent them from learning and
practicing the principles of Freemasonry. Men who speak languages other
than English often satisfy these requirements. Indeed , the spread of Masonry around the globe has demonstrated that its principles may be taught and
learned in many languages other than English.
. N.evertheless, ~ur law currently requires that, unless a Lodge has
historically used a different language in its degrees, the uniform ritual of this
Grand Lodge must be presented in English. Unfortunately, the exclusive
reliance upon English for the conferral degrees has the practical effect of
excluding from our Lodges candidates who are good men and true but
'
whose primary language is not English.
We believe that this exclusion will be an increasing problem for our
fraternity. Some six million Californians are Spanish speakers, among
whom there are undoubtedly many tens of thousands potential members.
The prohibition against the conferral of degrees in languages other than
~nglish discourages them to seek fraternal membership in our Lodges. and
instead encourages them to seek fraternal membership in clandestine
Lodges operating in Spanish.
Allowing a Lodge, such as Maya Lodge, to confer its degrees in Spanish
would have the advantages of (1) extending the benefits of Masonic member~hip to men who might otherwise remain as strangers to our fraternity,
(2) increasing t~e size and vitality of our Lodges by reaching out to a large
of i:x>tential members, and (3) strengthening our Grand Lodge by
d1souraging membership in clandestine Lodges.

P?°

In today's c osmopolitan society, if Masonry is to embrace all qualified
~en in our. jur.isdiction, then it must embrace more than one language.
~mce Spanish 1s overwhelmingly the largest minority language In the state.
rt makes sense that our first experimental steps into the presentation of our
ritual in those other languages should be taken in Spanish.

state that the Grand Lecturer must approve the translation of the ritual before

The Committee on Ritual:
Experience has demonstrated to the Committee on Ritual that the
presence of cipher rituals at practices is not disruptive to the conduct of
those meetings. On the contrary, their controlled use enhances the education process. Therefore, we were ready to support this legislation last year
until we noticed that it contained nothing which would prevent an officer who
is exemplifying our ritual at a school from simply reading it from the cipher
book.
We asked the proponent to resubmit again this year, but with that flaw
corrected . He has done so and we now unreservedly encourage your "Yes"
· vote.

The legislation as distributed to the Constituent Lodges is adequate to
carry out the intent of the proponents.
This Resolution seeks to amend our law and a 5/6 affirmative vote is
required for adoption.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
In 1988, cipher rituals were approved for possession and use in California. The proponent of this Resolution seeks to clarify the language added
to CMC 2688 by defining permissible conditions for their use.
The last sentence of CMC 2688 states that "In no event, however, shall
any cipher ritual be used during a tiled meeting."
Carry-over Resolution 90-28 also addressed the question of the use of
cipher rituals at practice sessions. The distiction between tiled meetings
and practice sessions was discussed in our report on that Resolution.
In Resolution 91-41 , the proponent wishes to add additional restrictions
that would permit the use of the cipher to those not participating in the
presentation of the ritual.
It is the Committee's opinion that the policy has been adequately
established in CMC 2688 and that additional exceptions and conditions are
necessary.
We recommend a "No" vote.

Therefore, we support legislation to remove this well-intentioned, but
obviously outdated. annotaion and recommend a "Yes" vote.
Resolution ADOPTED.

The legislation as distributed to the Constituent Lodges is adequate to
carry out the intent of the proponents.
This Resolution seeks to amend our law and our Ritual and a 5/6
affirmative vote is required for adoption.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
We are all aware that the purpose of divesting a candidate of all minerals
and metals is to teach him important Masonic lesson . If however, he is
unable to remove a ring due to enlargement of the finger thereby prohibiting
removal, or if he wears a prothesis containing metal, then exceptions are
permissible according to present law.

OF YOUNGER MEMBERS

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
At the One Hundred Fortieth Annual Communication of the Grand
Lodge, Most Worshipful Stanley L. Channon proposed in his Rec ommendation No. 20 that a Grand Lodge Committee on Conferences of Younger
Members be appointed. Most Worshipful Channon proposed that this
committee organize one or more conferences of Masons under forty-five
years of age at which these younger Masons would have an opportunity to

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

discuss ways and means of redirecting the Lodges and th~ir progr~ms. It
was also Grand Master Channon's recommendation that this committee be
composed of Masons under forty-five years of age.

alternate proficiency system where self study regarding the philosophy and
principles of Freemasonry could be emphasized rather than memorization
of answers to questions. Some noted the programs developed by Nebraska
and Illinois in whose alternate proficiency systems the candidate learns the
signs, words and modes of recognition and studies the philosophy of
Freemasonry through personal reading and group meetings, at the conclusion of which an open book examination is completed covering many of
the same areas of our current proficiencies but the greater depth and in the
candidate's own words. It was suggested that Grand Lodge consider the
appointment of a committee to study these alternate systems of candidate
proficiency with a view to adopting any of the advantages noted.

280

Most Worshipful Sam M. Pavlovich appointed us to the committee, and
we were reappointed by Most Worshipful Ronald A. Sherod for the current
year. Six conferences were held: Saturday, April 28, 1990 at the Fres~
Scottish Rite Cathedral, Saturday , May 5, 1990 at the San Jose Masonic
Temple, Saturday, May 19, 1990 at the Los Angeles Scottish Rite Cathedral,
Saturday, February 23, 1991 at the San Diego Scottish Rite, Saturday, March
2 1991 at the Sacramento Scottish Rite and Saturday, March 9, 1991 at the
Masonic Temple on Broadway in Oakland. Those in atten_danc~ we_re
enthusiastic and very interested in the future of Fr_eemas~nry 1n California.
Some traveled great distances to attend. All had ideas with respe_ct to the
future direction of Grand Lodge and our local Lodges. Four topics were
discussed: How can we encourage young men to become Masons? W~t
programs should Lodges otter? How can we interest young people 1n
leadership roles? For what should Masons be noted or ''what do Masons
do?"
This report will summarize the results of the conferences held in the past
two years.

How can We Encourage Young men to Become Masons?
Several concerns were noted in discussions of this_ question. Many
young men have limited amounts of additional time available for fraternal
activities because of work and other family commit~ents. Many yo~ng
wives work. It is difficult to interest many young men 1n fraternal o~ga~1z~­
tions unless families are involved and time devoted t~ the organizat10~ s
activities is used in the most effective manner possible. !he follo~ing
suggestions were made. All Lodge activities other than tiled meetings
should include families. The programs should be d~sig~ to interes~ _not
only Masons but their wives, children and non-Masonic fnends and fam11t~s.
Child care should be provided by the Lodge for younger people attending
Lodge activities with small children. Activities of interest to younger peo~le,
such as sports teams, should be encouraged. We should be more act~e
with the masonic youth groups. Some suggested that fewer lodges with
larger memberships wo uld have the people and funds to sponsor more
interesting programs.
Some but certainly not all participants questioned whether our present
system of candidate's proficiencies is the most effective use of the
candidate's time. Perhaps the same amount of time could be devoted to an

281

It was also suggested that Freemasonry is not sufficiently visible in the
community and that many young people are more interested in joining
groups which are community oriented. This area is discussed in greater
detail later in this report. Some also expressed that belief that the perceived
lack of ethnic and religious diversity in Freemasonry inhibits some young
people from joining. It was suggested that both Lodges and Grand Lodge
should have more qualified minority members in leadership roles.
Many felt that our members are unclear as to the limitations with respect
to our anti-solicitation rules. We should do a better job of educating our own
members about what may be said regarding the fraternity and how the
subject of membership may be approached with non-members without
violating our anti-solicitation rules.
Most importantly, many suggested that, in order to attract young
people, young people must be active and visible in the fraternity. Each
Lodge should organize a nucleus of its younger members to plan programs
to attract their contemporaries to Lodge activities. Many Lodges have
younger members who are no longer active. They should be recruited to
chair some social activities of the lodge which they and their non-Masonic
friends would attend with other members of the Lodge. Most people join a
group because of a present member whom they know. Unless younger
people are active in Lodges, other young people are not as likely to join.
Each Lodge should make an eHort to recruit younger people who are already
members to be more active in order to attract their friends. Encourage these
younger but perhaps presently inactive members to plan a social event in
which they might be interested and invite their friends, whether members or
not, to attend . They and their friends might thereby become more interested
in the fraternity.

282

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

What Programs Should Lodges Offer?
Many complained that Lodges repeat the same programs year after year
without much change or imagination in their presentation. A variety in
programming is important if Lodges are to attract and keep members,
regardless of age. The traditional programs can be popular year after year
if the content is varied and the event is professionally planned and conducted. For example, every Lodge should have an annual public schools
week program. There are a variety of activities which can be emphasized
at a public schools week program. Different ones might be chosen each
year. Those who plan the event should design the program to be of interest
to themselves and others who attend rather than doing the minimum
required. To encourage participation by younger members and keep the
interest of older members, Lodges should plan programs which appeal to
a broad age group. When such events are planned, Lodge officers should
make an extra effort to make each person present feel welcome. A greeters
committee might be useful. The Lodge leadership should spend time with
as many people present as possible and encourage others to do likewise.
Many present felt that Masonic education does not have a sufficiently
prominent role in many Lodges' programming. Masonic education may be
planned not only for tiled meetings but for stated meeting dinners and other
events where families are present. Additional services from Grand Lodge
might be useful. Grand Lodge should consider an investment in recording
equipment to produce video and audio cassette tape masters of presentations on Masonic topics and arrange with outside providers to duplicate
these tapes. The candidate system of education was suggested as a
program which could be improved with companion video and audio cassette tape presentations. Each Lodge should be encouraged to have its
own television set and video cassette recorder. The newer members, their
wives and families could be encouraged to come to the Lodge or a member's
home to view the video presentation and then participate in a discussion
with perhaps more experienced members present. The audio cassette
tapes could be lent for use in the car by candidates and other members
while commuting.
How Can We Interest Young People in Leadership Roles?
Again, the time commitment was the most often voiced concern. It was
suggested that more qualified young people might aspire to leadership roles
in Lodges if the administrative and ritualistic functions of the Master, Wardens and Senior Deacon were separated, with the Master, Wardens and
Senior Deacon of the Lodge serving as administrative officers and separate
officers available to confer the degrees and give the lectures when requested

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

283

to do so. Some suggested that the administration of the Lodges and
presentation of the ritual might improve if specialists were responsible for
each.
Some suggested that more young people would aspire to Lodge
leadership roles if we had better program to educate them in not only what
was expected of them in those roles but how they could plan an effective
program. More leadership training is needed. While many present were
not aware of the Grand Lodge Wardens' Retreats program, many felt that
more programs of that type were needed. Lodge line officers need practical
information on how to plan interesting programs. For all Masonic leaders,
both you and old, Grand Lodge should increase its emphasis on proper
leadership training.
In summary, if the Master, Wardens and Senior Deacon can concentrate
their efforts on leading the Lodge and planning its programs. with the ability
to delegate ritualistic responsibilities to others, and if the Grand Lodge
increases its assistance in training local Lodge leaders in planning programs
that have been successful elsewhere, more young people might be interested in committing the time required to accept leadership roles .
For What Should Masons be Noted or "What Do Masons Do?"
We must do a better job of practicing in the community our Masonic
tenets of brotherly love. relief and truth. We must not simply profess our
Masonic teachings by our words but by our actions among those around
us, whether affiliated with Masonry or not. Lodges must be more visible in
the community. Masons should not be known just for attend ing meetings
among themselves but for what they do in the community. Each Lodge
should be encouraged to identify needs in its own community and work to
address them. Many familiar with the California Masonic Code expressed
a desire to amend Section 2316 to permit Lodge funds to be used for
non-Masonic charities.
Masonry is the world's oldest and largest fraternity becau se of its
unique. philosophical content. Masonry can again attract young people
with its philosophical content if we put its tenets into everyday practice
brotherly regard for every human being with whom we come in contact. relief
or charity for those less fortunate than we. regardless of their affiliation with
the fraternity, and truth, the practice of those timeless teachings by which
we hope to fit ourselves as perfect stones in a better super-structure of
society. If we can practice and demonstrate these tenets outside th e Lodge

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

through our Masonic activities in the community, not only will we fulfill better
our responsibUities as Masons but certainly we will attract others, both young
and old, to join with us.

While some of the items mentioned in this report would require changes
in the California Masonic Code or other actions by the Grand Lodge, many
may be done by local Lodge initiative. Many at the conferences concluded
that these ideas could be implemented in their Lcx:lges without Grand Lcx:lge
Help and that it only took one person, each person present, to return to his
Lcx:lge to start. Many left renewed in their enthusiasm for the fraternity and
his place in its future success.
The committee recommends that the format of these conferences by
changed in the future. instead of inviting o~y members under the age of
forty-five, invite all members, regardless of age, and perhaps their families
also to a town meeting on the craft where issues of concern to those in
attendance may be discussed with appropriate representatives from the
Grand Lodge. Grand Lodge leadership will gather possible programs for
the improvement of the fraternity and will leave with a better appreciation of
the concerns of the craft for the future of the fraternity. The craft will sense
that Grand lodge leadership is concerned about their ideas and leave with
renewed enthusiasm for the future of the fraternity. Perhaps these sessions
can be held when the Grand Master will otherwise be in an area and can be
done without the expense of this committee.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:

The Investment Committee has the responsibility of reporting of annually to Grand Lodge on the condition of the various funds of Grand Lodge and
those of its entities.
During the year quarterly meetings are held by the Committee with is
Investment counselors. At each meeting an independent analytical consulting firm reviews the performance of the various funds as compared with
similar funds, ie., endowment, non-profit and trust funds, in the United
States.
The primary concern of the Committee is the preservation of the
principal of the various funds together with the highest rate of return
commensurate with safety and good investment practice.
Three funds, Masonic Homes Endowment Fund, Masonic Homes
General Fund and the Hugo M. Lorber Union City Fund constitute 95% of
the total investments.
Among other funds supervised by the Committee are the General Fund
of Grand Lodge, the funds of the California Masonic Memorial Temple,
California Masonic Foundation and Amaranth, Pooled Income and several
restricted-use ·funds of Masonic Homes.
As of August 20, 1991 , the Investment Committee accepted the respon sibility for the oversight of the investment of the funds in the Retirement Plan
from the Retirement Committee. Effective October 1, 1991, the funds have
been allocated to two separate managers who are specialists respectively
in fixed Income and equities.
The market value of the total portfolio on June 30, 1991 was
$271 ,385,400 compared to $261, 129,000 a year earlier, an increase of 3.9%.
The 1990-1991 cash yield from the total invested funds was 6. 7%.
Fixed income securities, including government and corporate bonds
composed 63% of the total portfolio. The remainder consisted of common
stocks and cash equivalents.
The Pooled Income Fund is of particular importance to the Masonic
Homes. On June 30, 1991, the Fund had a market value of $4,517,887. The
cash yield was 8.19%. The Pooled income Fund gives Masons and others

286

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

in California the opportunity to create a lifetime income for themselves and
for one-time designated beneficiaries. Certain tax advantages may accrue
to the contributor. Eventually, the Masonic Homes becomes the final
beneficiary.

1. We revised the Grand Master's Achievement Award form and the
eligibility point system to bring more equity to the smaller lodges.
This year we reviewed and approved over 170 Grand Master

The rewarding accumulation of assets in the various funds of Grand
Lodge has been the result of the efforts of Masons and their friends. The
operations of the Masonic Homes at Union City and Covina are financed
almost entirely from through the income from the Endowment and General
Fund investments. The expansion at Union City in the last several years was
funded entirely from the Hugo M. Lorber Fund. Other revenues furnish
support for the charitable activities and educational grants of the Grand
Lodge of California.

2. We have continued to promote the committee's "Lodge Leadership Handbook" for improvement and better access to lodge officers.

The Funds' investments rank among the highest in quality because the
Investment Committee exercises the utmost prudence and care in their
overseeing of the management of the funds. The cash yield and the total
return have been satisfactory in view of the Committee's conservative
investment policy and the securities markets.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Income from the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund amounted to
$6,885,840 which was transferred to the operating accounts of the Masonic
Homes of California. This income is an extremely vital and important factor
in providing the Hornes' Trustees with a portion of the funds necessary to
maintain the exceptionally high quality of health care and services afforded
to the residents. Another use of th is income is to help provide nonresidential
assistance for those who are not able to become a resident. This income
also assists in providing money for present as well as future construction
and enhancement of the facilities at our Hornes.

REFLECTIONS
The Masonic Homes Endowment Fund fiscal year of 1990-1991 was one
of ups and downs. Considering the state of the economy, the demands
placed on our money available for contribution to other charities, and our
continued decline in membership, we are grateful for what we have
achieved.
The programs that were instituted three years ago to increase the
awareness of the Masonic Homes in the members of our Fraternity are
continuing to show positive results.
The presentation of the book "The Greatest of These is Charity" -- a
history of the Masonic Homes of California -- is being widely accepted as
one of great enlightenment to both the new Entered Apprentice as well as
the seasoned Master Mason. Lodges can receive these books by contacting their Endowment Board member who will be pleased to make the
presentation to the new Entered Apprentice.
The response to the Masonic Homes Endowment lapel Pins and the
Appreciation Certificates is continuing to be strong. The lapel Pin for 1992
is quite different and should appeal to our contributors. It is in the shape of
the map of California.
There are many pluses in the contributions of 1990-1991. In deference
to the state of the economy, we are pleased to report that the average
contribution per contributor increased to $20.64, and the percentage of

295

Also of interest is the fact that of the six divisions in the jurisdiction , two
of them had increases in contributions. Division II and Division VI had
increases of 10.9% and 2.3% respectively. Interestingly enough, these two
areas are economically different and at the opposite ends of the state.
Another point of interest is that over 50% of the Lodges increased their
contributions over the prior year. However, the Lodges with increases were
not of sufficient magnitude to offset the decrease in contributions from the
Lodges.

PLANNING FOR THE FUTURE

There is a major issue that needs serious attention and help from the
Brethren. "How can we reach the Brethren who do not now contribute to
the Endowment Fund and convince them to help in the support of our
Homes?" We often hear that many of our Brethren can't afford to contribute
because they are retired and on fixed incomes. We are sure that some of
our Brethren are in that condition but not 53% of our members! Even small
contributions are solicited . Just think, if every member contributed the price
of a cup of coffee each month, every Lodge would achieve Honor Roll. If
any one has any idea of how to solve this problem, please contact any
Endowment Board member and make your ideas known.

The lnd.ivi~ual Contribution Incentive Program is progressing very well
and. the ma1o_nty of ~he Lodges are participating in the program. We have
designed a b~llfold sized P!astic calendar for 1992. On the side opposite to
th.e calendar is the Masonic emblem and inscription, "It's up to you in 92 __
Grve to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund."
A number in excess of the membership of each Lodge was sent to the
Secretary of each Lodge with the hope that they will be included in the dues
envelope to each Mason in California. Hopefully, we will convince the 53%
of our members to contribute something to the support of the Endowment
Fund .
. We still have discrepancies in the reporting and recording of contributions a~ the number of contributors for Honor Roll recognition. Here is a
sugge~t1on -- How about making the check payable to the "California
Mas~rnc Homes Endowment Fund" and in the "Memo" section on the lower
left side of the check indicate the number of contributors. Think about it
that would be a permanent record!!
·
The Endowment Board is constantly reviewing the Masonic Homes
pamphlets to be sure that they are up to date and reflect current programs.
Last year the pamphlets were completely redesigned and we have received
many compliments. Lodges are encouraged to dispose of obsolete
pamphlets and order from the new ones because the information contained
in them may leave the wrong impressions and impact our Endowment Fund
Program.
In planning the printing budget each year we look at the historical orders
of pamphlets from the Lodges. One way that Lodges can help the Board
and to have up to date pamphlets, is to order only the quantity of dues
envelopes and pamphlets that it intends to use in one year.

T~e.~resentation of the book "The Greatest of These is Charity" to the
newly initiated Entered Apprentice has been a great success. The Board of
Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California are in favor of continuing the
progra~ and ~re_ en.th~siastic supporters of the program. There are many
Lodges in the JUnsd1et1on that still do not avail themselves of this program.
Our B~rd members will endeavor to see that each newly initiated Entered
Appre~t1ce has the opportunity to receive a copy of the history of the
Masonic Homes of California.

will be presented to the Lodge during the Annual Communication by a
member of the Endowment Board.
