PROCEEDINGS OF THE

EPILOGUE
Our sincere and grateful thanks to Grand Master Ronald A. Sherod and
to the Grand Lodge Officers, Board Members and Committeemen for their
support of the Endowment Program. We also wish to thank the Masters.
Wardens, Secretaries and especially the Lodge Endowment Fund Chairmen
for their efforts in furthering this worthy program.
We also extend a very special thanks to the 66,178 Brothers who,
through their continued generosity, contributed over one and a third million
dollars to the Endowment Fund during this fiscal year.
We appreciate the splendid assistance and support we have received
from the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees, the Grand Secretary's office
under the leadership of the Very Worshipful Robert A. Klinger. Bob, just a
personal note from the Board, we will really miss you and offer you and
Marilyn our very best wishes for the future. And to all of the staff of the Grand
Lodge Office a hearty thanks for all your help.
Once again I wish to offer my personal thanks to the Homes Endowment
Board Members for their dedication and devotion in the support extended
to me again during this past year as your Chairman. With all the new
demands presented to them, they have continued to respond with vigor and
enthusiasm and their response Is most gratifying. It trul y is the great people
of the Endowment Board who work so diligently that ensures the success
of our program.
My special thanks goes to Chuck Grossman, Wilber Holtzclaw, Nelson
Bartoo and Leroy Ervin. They have served with distinction and are now
leaving the Board.
Respectfully submitted,
John M. "Jack" Palmer, Chairman

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:

Public Schools: Working For the Present - Ensuring the Future

Sll. 79
'20.~

With the above Public Schools Week theme for 1991, the Grand Lodge
Committee on Public Schools continued to operate under the "Memorandum of Understanding" issued by Past Grand Master the Most Worshipful
Stanley L. Channon, which delineated specific responsibilities of the Substance Abuse Prevention Program to various Grand Lodge Cornmitt.ees.
Primarily, the Public Schools Committee was charged with the responsibility
for developing procedures to use in order to apply for funding of proposal
under this program. Furthermore, this Committee was designated to
receive and review the school systems' funding applications and recommend those deserving support to the California Masonic Foundation.
Because of the amount of available funds, the Committee continued to
work with and receive superb support from the County/State Steering
Committee (CSSC), an adjunct of the Association of County Superintendents of Schools, in enacting these responsibilities. Clearly, this cooperation has realized many new friends for Masonry. Countless expressions of
gratitude have been communicated to the Grand Lodge.
The amount recommended for distribution again showed a substantial
increase: $149 ..449, as opposed to $114,000 for last year. The amount was
awarded to the ten Healthy Kids Regional Centers, ensuring that all public
school systems would benefit from the awards. These centers are jointly
established by the State of California's Department of Education and the
several County Offices of Education. Every effort was made to involve those
included in the "memorandum of understanding, " the Lodges. District Inspectors, Committeemen, and other members of the Masonic family. Some
work still remains in order to attain optimum involvement of the fraternity,
schools, and general public.
With the increase of the Committee for 30 to 50 members, there was a
noted increase in Committee activity in other areas of its responsibility.
There were many reports of excellent Public Schools' Week Observances from throughout the State covering such activities as scholarship
awards. recognition of student and staff excellence, and even a "shootout"
and dramatic skit at a historical "gold country" community in the Sierra
Foothills.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

It was evident that many Lodges are aggressively implementing creative
ideals in linking with their local schools.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON TEMPLE PROPERTIES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lcxige, F.& A.M. of California:

The Committee on Temple Properties and Taxation is pleased to submit
the following annual report of its activities for the 1990-1991 Masonic Year:

317

Again this was the number one subject of the inquiries to our members
and for activities of the members in working with the Temple Boards.
Compliance with the California Masonic Code, sections 2304 and 2305, on
the required use of the "Uniform By-Laws" and the periodic return of funds
above those necessary to operate the Temple Boards to the ownership
lodges to hold in trust have been foremost in our efforts.
The Committee has been more aggressive In calling upon the administrative arm of the Grand Lodge, the Inspectors, to enforce the
provisions of the California Masonic Code. as they relate to the Temple
Associations within their various administrative districts. The chairman has
meet with Inspectors at their schools in the Third, Fourth, Fifth and Sixth
Divisions and was represented at the schools for the First Division, where
these roles were discussed.
Financial Reporting
Tne most recent reports to the Grand Lodge from the Temple Associations indicate that the financial health of many of the Temple Boards are
"ailing". Of concern, the decline In number of tenants renting the Temple
Association buildings on an on-going basis as a result of mergers, dwindling
numbers of youth and ladies groups and the fewer lodges remaining as
tenants. Recent changes in the Masonic Law on "outside rentals" have not
yet had their full impact on the Temple Associations, but are making our
facUies more competitive in price. This development will be monitored
closely in the coming years and reported to you.
Committee Reorganization
The Committee has undergone a very basic reorganization, with the
addition of the duties of the former Special Committee on Taxation. The
membership has been learning the complexities of the tax codes and the
situations that our lodges and our temples face yearly in meeting and
fufilling the requirements thereof. This appears to be another area of heavy
Impact upon the duties of the committeemen.
Committee Publication
In 1983, the Committee issued its "Handbook'', which has been in use
as a guide to the Lodges and Temples throughout the State. In 1990 the
revision of the "Handbook" was begun, and the 1990 annual communication
changed several of the areas of the proposed book.

318

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

An abbreviated edition of the future handbook has been used with much
praise in the sessions with the Inspectors, and with some area Temple
Associations. Until the full editing work can be agreed upon and completed
the abbreviated edition will "make do."

Workload
The Com~i~ee's workload is growing, as more of the Lodges and
Temple Assoc1at1ons come to a realization that there is help available in the
area co.mmitteeman, and that all they have to do is ask for it. In Temple
Properties alone, the workload has grown tremendously, with many of the
Temple projects requiring multi-year attention from the committeemen as
the work progresses; especially on the new temples that are being discussed
and proposed.
Special Thanks
The Committee expresses its appreciation on the Grand Lodge staff, the
Grand Secretary, Robert Klinger and his staff, and the members of the
Insurance Committee for their aid and assistance in the past year.
We certainly have appreciated the full support and assistance of the
Grand Master and Deputy Grand Master. their accessibility and rapid
responses to our requests. allowing us to communicate decisions to the
Lodges faster than ever before.
A special thanks is also given to the many Masters, Wardens. Presidents,
Ch~irmen, Temple Association Members and especially the Inspectors for
their thoughtful and considerate hearing of our problems and their constructive comments.

U.S. CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Locfge, F.& AM. of California:

The purpose of the Annual U.S. Constitution Observance celebration is
to honor the document that forms the basis of our national democracy and
our individual freedoms. As Masons, it becomes an opportunity to recall a
moment in history when 23 of the 39 signers of the U.S. Constitution were
Masons. The Grand Lodge of California encourages each lodge to openly
celebrate the anniversary of this document in September with a patriotic
program and further encourages the lodges to invite the public.
The U.S. Constitution Observance Committee is organized to support
the lodges in California as a resource for planning and assisting with the U.S.
Constitution Observance programs. Using several methods to organize
earty planning efforts. some committeemen wrote to the Masters of the
lodges, some telephones the Masters, a few visited the lodges directly, and
others attended the District schools of Instruction. Additionally, the committee sponsored booths at the Annual Grand Lodge Communication and
at most of the Officer Administrative Seminars conducted around the state.
The booths were decorated with display materials to get lodge officers to
think about their U.S. Constitution Observance program plans and to get
them to take free samples/supplies for the programs.

.

As a result of the above methods of lodge contact to promote early
planning, many of the lodges included the committeemen on their U.S.
Constitution Observance Committees and, in a couple of cases. the committeemen acted as Chairmen for the lodge committees. In giving assistance with the programs, many of the committeemen provided display
materials, several advised and some acquired speakers or other entertainment for the programs, a few became speakers (themselves) for the
programs, and a small number acted as hosts for the programs.
A sampling throughout California by the U.S. Constitution Observance
committeemen, indicate that more than 90% of the lodges held a program.
Sixty-six percent of the programs featured a speaker. Among the speakers
were current Grand Lodge Officers, past Grand Lodge Officers, U.S. Congressmen, California Assemblymen, judges, attorneys, a Dean of a Law
School and a Sheriff. Almost 40% of the programs were oriented to entertainment such as plays by various Scottish Rite Bodies. picnics and barbecues, U.S. Flag programs, a parade, a high school essay contest, a high
school debate, a Daughter's of the American Revolution play, and a citizenship program co-sponsored by the U.S. Naturalization and Immigration

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Service. Most of these programs, approximately 75%, were held as special
events on special days or evenings. The remainder were included with the
dinner and activities of the Stated Meeting.

MORNING SESSION - WEDNESDAY

The majority of lodges now seem to be combining their programs with
at least one other lodge, and many have combined to form district or
multi-district programs. These larger programs were the best advertised
and received the greatest public support.

At 9:00 a.m. Grand Lodge was called on with the Grand Master presiding. This session of the Annual Communication was raised by Ronald C.
Perry, Junior Warden of Catalina Island Lodge No. 524 using the gavel
presented for two cornerstone laying ceremonies in Santa Maria. Other
gavels used during this morning session had been presented to the Grand
Master at the annual Western Bar-b-que at Davis listed by the 21 Oth Masonic
District and at a reception for him by Bell Lodge No. 483 and the 592nd
Masonic District.

INSTALLATION OF OFFICERS
With Past Grand Master Donald B. McCaw acting as Installing Officer
and Past Grand Master Roy J. Henville acting as Master of Ceremonies, the
appointive officers were individually introduced and collectively installed in
their respective offices. The Grand Lecturer, Grand Secretary and Grand
Treasurer were then individually introduced and together were installed,
following which the Junior and Senior Grand Wardens were introduced and
installed. Following the installation of the Deputy Grand Master, Gloria
Cazneaux, the wife of the Grand Master-elect, offered a vocal solo, "Once
in a Lifetime." Following the ceremony of installation of the Grand Master,
she again sang a solo, "The Lord's Prayer." She was accompanied for both
solos by Constance Torrey, organist. The newly appointed and installed
Grand Chaplain addressed the assemblage with a short talk entitled "law of

which was received with a thunderous and prolonged round of applause.

Past Grand Master Ronald A. Sherod, with a gift on behalf of the Grand
Lodge and Past Grand Master Sherod was presented with his Past Grand
Master's apron, lapel pin and certificate attesting to his status by Past Grand
Masters Stanley L. Channon, John W. Driskell and Leo B. Mark respectively.
Past Grand Master Sherod appropriately responded.
Grand Master Cazneaux called on each newly installed Grand Lodge
Officer who in turn introduced the members of their respective families who
were present. He then accepted several gifts from members of his familyone of which was the gavel he had received in 1976 when he was installed

INDEPENDENT AUDITORS' REPORT

To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of
Free and Accepted Masons of the
State of California
San Francisco, California
We have audited the accompanying balance sheet of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of
Free and Accepted Masons of the State of Califo rnia (a nonprofit, unincorporated fraternal
organization) at June 30, 1991 and the related statement of support, revenue and expenses
and chanses in fund balance for the year then ended. These fi nancial statements a re the
responsibility o f the Grand Lodge's management. Our responsibility is to express an o pinion
on these financia l statements and supplemental schedules based on our audit. The Grand
Lodge's financial statements as of June 30, 1990 were audited by other auditors whose report
dated September IO, 1990 expressed an unqualified opinion on those statements.
We conducted our audit in accorda nce with generally accepted auditing standards. Those
standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about
whether the financial statements arc free of material misstatement. An audit includes
examining, on a test basis, evidence supporting the amounts and disclosures in the finan cial
statements. An audit also includes assessing the accounting principles used and significant
estimates made by management, as well as evaluating the ove rall financial statement
presentation. We believe that our audit provides a reasonable basis for our opinion.
In our opinion, such financial statements present fairly , in all ma terial respects, the financial
position of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of
California at June 30, 1991 and the results of its operations a nd changes in fund balance for
the year then ended in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles.
Our audit was conducted for the purpose of forming an opinion on the basic financial
statements taken as a whole. The supplemental schedules appearing on pages 8 through 12
arc presented for the purpose of additional analysis and arc not a required part of the b asic
financial statements. The supplemental schedules arc the responsibility of the Grand
Lod,ge's management. Such 1991 supplemental schedules have been subjected to the
auditing procedures arplied in the audit of the basic fin a ncial statements and, in our opinion,
are fairly stated in al material respects when considered in relation to the basic financial
statements taken as a whole.

Orianjz.atjon • The Grand Lod~e is an unincorporated association and is governed by a
constitution and ordinances setting fonh its jurisdiction and authority. The jurisdiction of
the Grand Lodge includes all lodges and Masons within the state of California, and
members of lodges of California, wherever residing.
The Lodge provides general and administrative services to its related entities: the
Masonic H omes of Califo rnia (Masonic Homes), the California Masonic Memorial
Temple (Temple), the California Masonic Foundation (Foundation), and the California
Masonic R etirement Plan.
Revenue Recoinitjon · Per-capita revenue from lodges is recognized as income on its
assessment date, June 30.
Inventory is stated at cost.
Investments in marketable securities are stated at fair market value and, to the extent that
management intends to hold such investments for more than one year, arc classified as
noncurrent assets. Gains or losses that result [rom market fluctuations are recognized in
the period such fluctuat ions occur. Realized sains or losses resulting from sales or
maturiticS of securities are calculated on an adjusted cost basis. Adjusted cost is the
market value of the security at the beginning of the year, or cost if purchased during the
year.
Prorcrty and e~ ui pme nt are recorded at <:ost and arc dep reciated o n the straight-line
met od over estimated useful lives of three to twenty-five yea rs.

BEQUEST
Jn 1990, the Grand Lodge received $370,317 from the Estate.of Jack I. MacKechnie. The
total received, p lus accrued interest of $2,367, was included m deferred revenue pending
legal clarification regarding the use of the income from the Estate. In 1991 the matter
was resolved and $370,317 was transferred from deferred revenue to bequest revenue. In
1991, the Grand Lodge received final distributions of $7,985. To comply with ~e
provisions of Mr. MacKechnie's will, the inc-0me has been transferred to the Masonic
Foundation to be used to provide scholarships for needy high school graduates of proven
outstanding athletic ability. The bequest has earned interest of $23,406 and $2,367
throuah June 30, 1991 and 1990, respectively. The related investments and cash are
incluaed in restricted fund balanc~.

INVENTORY

for resale to constituent lodges. Such inventory includes written pubhcatJons and other
materials related to the practice of Masonry. Previously all mvent<;>ry was expensed as
purchased. The effect of this change result~d in a reducuo~ of supplies expense for fiscal
year 1991 of approximately $1 88,000. Pno r year fi nancial statements have not been

Board of Trustees
Masonic Homes of California
San Francisco, California
We have audited the accompanying balance sheet of the Masonic Homes of California (a
California nonprofit corporation) at June 30, 1991 and the related statement of support,
revenue and expenses and changes in fund balances for the year then ended. These financial
statements are the responsibility of the Masonic Homes' management. Our responsibility is
to express an opinion on these financial statements based on our audit. The Maso nic
Homes' financial statements and supplemental schedules as of June 30, 1990were audited by
other auditors whose report dated September 13, 1990 eX'pressed an unqualified opinion on
those statements, totals of which arc included for comparative purposes only.
We conducted our audit in accordance with generally accepted auditing standards. Those
standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about
whether the financial statements arc free of material misstatement. An audit includes
examining, on a test basis, evidence supporting the amounts and disclosures in the financial
statements. An audit also includes assessing the accounting principles used and significant
estimates made by management, as well as evaluating the overall financial statement
presentation. We believe that our audit provides a reasonable basis for our opinion.
In our opinion, such financial statements present fairly, in all material respects, the financial
position of the Masonic Homes of Ca1ifornia at June 30, 1991 and the results of its
operations and changes in fund balances for the year then ended in conformity with generally
accepted accounting principles.
Our audit was conducted for the purpose of forming an opinion on the basic financial
statements taken as a whole. The supplemental schedules appearing on pages 8 throug.h 10
are pre.sented for the purpose of add1uonal analysis and are not a required part of the basic
financial statements. The supplemental schedules are the responsibility of the Masonic
Homes' management. Such 1991 supplemental schedules have been subjected to the
auditing procedures af plied in the audit of the basic financial statements and in our opinion,
are fairly stated in al material respects when considered in relation to the basic financial
statements taken as a whole.

The Masonic Homes Pooled Income Fund was organized in 1974 and is a charitable
remainder trust to which do nors contribute irrevocable remainder interests in propeny
while retaining an income interest for life for one or more beneficiaries. The donors arc
entitled to a tax deduction equivalent to the present value of the remainder interest in the
propeny contributed.

ORGANIZATION

The property tra nsferred by a donor is held in trust by the Board of Trustees of the
Masonic Homes Pooled Income Fund and is commingled with and invested and
reinvested with other properties transferred to the Fund. All dividend and interest
income of the Fund is distributed quarterly to the beneficiaries, based on their
proportionate share of the Pool. Upon the death of each donor's last income beneficiary,
the remainder interest is distributed to Masonic Homes of California, a charitable
corporation.

2.

SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES
Investments - Investments in marketable securities are reported at their fair market value.
Properties contributed during the year by donors are recorded at their fair market value
at date of receipt. Gains or losses resulting from sales or market fluctuations. are
recognized as adjustments to fund balance in the period such sales or market fluctuations
occur.

See notes to financial statements.

Administrative Costs - Administrative costs of the Pooled Income Fund totaling S45,339
in 1990 and $46,743 in 1989 are paid by the Masonic Homes of California.

3.

FEDERAL AND STATE INCOME TAXES
The Fund pays no income tax on income distributed to beneficiaries. Applicable federal
and state income taxes are paid by the beneficiaries on their share of distributed income.

4.

INVESTMENTS IN MARKETABLE SECURITIES
Investments at December 31, 1990 and 1989 are presented at fair market value and are
comprised of the following:

California M asonic Retirement Plan (the Plan) as of December 31, 1990, and the related

express an opinion on these financial statements based on our audit. The Plan's finan cial
statements for the year ended December 31, 1989 were audited by other auditors whose
report, dated June 21, 1990, expressed an unqualified opinion on those statements.
We conducted our audit in ac.cordance with generally accepted auditing standards. Those
standards require that we plan and perform the a udit to obtain reasonable assurance about
whet her the financial statements are fre e of materia l misstatement. An audit includes
examining, on a test basis, evidence supporting the amounts and disclosures in the financial
statements. An audit a lso includes assessing the acco unting principles used and significant
estimates made by management, as well as evaluating the overall financial statement
presentation. We believe that our audit provides a reasonable basis for our opinion.
In our opinion, such financial statements present fairly, in all material respects, the net assets
of the Plan at December 31, 1990 and the changes in its net assets for the year then ended in
conformity with generally accepted accounting principles.
Our audit was conducted for the purpose of forming an o pinion on t he basic financial

stated in all material respects when considere d in relation to the basic 1990 financial
